pdf_text.text: IOM Nigeria thanks the National Bureau of Statistics, National Emergency Management Agency, Gombe State Emergency Management Agency, the Nigerian Red Cross Society and other partners for their continued collaboration. Intention Survey is made possible with support from DTM NIGERIA IDP INTENTION SURVEY IN GOMBE STATE 15 April 2024 Nigeria north-east zone | Intention survey report Round 1 (April 2024) | 1 T wenty-seven per cent (27%)of respondents in both camps/camp-like settings and the host communities intend to return to their locations of origin. Fourty-seven per cent (47%) of respondents who intended to return to their place of origin stated that their houses were partially damaged and need repair. INTENTIONS TO RETURN Only three per cent of respondents in Gombe State intended to relocate to another LGA or state, but most of this group intended to relocate to other LGAs in the state. T wenty-/f_ive per cent (25%) of respondents indicated that the search for livelihood/income was the primary reason for their decision to relocate. INTENTIONS TO RELOCATE Sixty-four per cent (64%) of respondents who intended to integrate into the host community mentioned that the major reason for their decision was that the security situation was good in their current place of displacement. INTENTIONS TO INTEGRATE Fourty per cent (40%) of respondents in Gombe State stated that they did not intend to leave the locations where they are currently displaced in the coming months. They intend to integrate into the host communities. OVERALL KEY FINDINGS IN GOMBE STATE INTRODUCTION The north-east region of Nigeria grapples with a deeply intricate displacement crisis predominantly caused by human conflicts. The non-state armed groups (NSAGs) perpetuate violence, driving large-scale displacement, while climate change intensifies the existing conflict situations and displacement. Furthermore, the north-east region, which includes Yobe, Borno, Adamawa, Bauchi, Gombe, and Taraba states, faces significant exposure to natural calamities such as floods. The escalation of violence since 2014 triggered a multifaceted humanitarian emergency, leading to mass displacement across the area. This situation continues to this day, with the north-east still accommodating substantial numbers of internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees. While many of the IDPs continued to be displaced for prolonged periods, there is a noticeable trend of increasing numbers of IDPs returning to their places of origin, as evidenced by Round 45 of DTM assessments (June 2023) identified 2,075,257 returnees in the region. Recognizing the growing number of returnees, the IOM Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM)/Shelter and NFI and Protection sectors, including the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), Nigeria Red Cross Society (NRCS), and other key partners deemed it necessary to assess the future intentions (within the next 12 months) of individuals in displacement areas to provide appropriate solution interventions. The DTM of the IOM Nigeria Mission, with the support of the partners, led the Intention Survey (IS) in Gombe State (including the other five states of the north-east) to assess IDPs who wish to return to their place of origin, locally integrate at their current location of displacement or relocate to another part of the state (LGA), within or outside the country. Out of the 8,262 displaced households in Gombe, a total of 2,898 households (in the host communities) were interviewed as a sample to determine their intentions towards a preferred solution (return, relocate or integrate) within the next 12 months. The goal was (1) to ensure a safe and dignified return to their places of origin, (2) to assist the integration of IDPs in the location of displacement, and (3) to support local relocation. By shedding light on the IDP’s future intentions, which are often influenced by security conditions and livelihood prospects in the selected locations of solutions, this report seeks to provide a better understanding of the decision-making process of internally displaced individuals regarding their future homes linked to return, local relocation or integration and the conditions necessary for sustainable solutions following their intentions, thereby, generating advocacy, policy related discussions and decision-making in line with the protection-centred approaches. OBJECTIVES The Intention Survey tool aims to collect detailed data about the IDPs wishing to be on a path towards solutions within the next 12 months. The main objectives of the survey are as follows: I. T o assess IDPs who wish to return, relocate, and locally integrate. II. T o map out areas to which IDPs wish to return, relocate, and locally integrate. III. T o underst and the conditions in (actual and intended) locations of solutions. IV. T o determine the estimated timelines f or return, relocation, and local integration. 1National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), Gombe State Emergency Management Agencies (SEMA), National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) and Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS) IDP INTENTION SURVEY — NORTH EAST NIGERIA GOMBE STATE ROUND 1 Nigeria north-east zone | Intention survey report Round 1 (April 2024) DISCLAIMER The opinions expressed in the report are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the International Organization for Migration (IOM). IOM expresses no opinion concerning the legal status of any country, territory, city or area, or of its authorities, or concerning its frontiers or boundaries. iomnigeriadtm@iom.intdtm.iom.int/nigeria METHODOLOGY IOM strictly followed the UN General Assembly Guidelines when planning and conducting this survey. While the UN General Assembly Guidelines are mainly addressed to states, they also explicitly apply to personal data files kept by governmental and international organizations, including IOM. The key principles of the guidelines are lawfulness and fairness, accuracy, interested- person access, non-discrimination, purpose-specification, proportionality, respect for the data subject’s rights, security and confidentiality, and accountability and supervision. The execution of this survey, including the methodology, scope, and presentation of the findings in this report, adhered to global best practices as outlined by the IOM Global DTM toolkit. Quantitative research methods were employed to formulate the interview questionnaire and implement the survey. In preparation for the questionnaire, consultations were organized with the CCCM/NFI/Shelter and the protection sectors. Following the sessions, DTM tested the survey instrument by conducting ten pilot interviews (5 households per population strata) per state. The final survey questionnaire was comprised of eight (8) open-ended questions, 158 closed questions (closed questions are queries eliciting a “yes” or “no” response), and 17 semi-closed questions. After the finalization of the questionnaire, enumerators and partners (36) in Gombe State were trained by the IOM DTM. Data was entered into the DTM Kobo server after face-to-face interviews, which was then processed for the analytical report. Although the term “voluntary return” is not reflected in the questionnaire, interviewers were trained and instructed to explain to each interviewee that survey questions relate to returns of a voluntary nature only. The meaning of each solution—voluntary return, integration, and relocation was explained to each interviewee. DTM staff monitored interviews to verify that these concepts were clearly introduced and well understood. This survey, conducted in Yobe state, contributed to the analysis of the intention of the two surveyed population groups: IDPs dispersed in camp/camp-like settings are persons who have been forced to leave their homes or places of habitual residence and reside in a formal or informal camp. IDPs dispersed in host communities are persons who have been forced to leave their homes or places of habitual residence and live with the local residents. The intention survey’s sampling framework relied on the DTM Mobility Tracking Round 45 (Sep 2023) dataset. This data provided a breakdown of the IDP populations at administrative level 4 (location/sites), which formed the sample frame for the survey. The Intention Survey used a two-stage cluster sampling. The primary sampling units in the first stage were the IDP sites, as identified by the Mobility Tracking Assessment Round 45. In the second stage, households were randomly interviewed from the identified IDP sites. Out of the 8,262 displaced households in Gombe, a total of 2,898 households (in the host communities) were interviewed to determine their preferred durable solution within the next 12 months. /reports/nigeria-heavy-rainfall-flash-re.title: Nigeria — Heavy Rainfall Flash Report Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno and Gombe states (28 August 2024)
/reports/nigeria-heavy-rainfall-flash-re.summary: Between 18 and 25 August 2024, northern Nigeria experienced severe storms and heavy rainfall, resulting in widespread displacement across the region. The impact was felt most acutely in Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno, and Gombe states. In Adamawa, Numan LGA was hit the hardest as well, where a staggering 1,009 households and 5,844 individuals were impacted by the floodwaters. Madagali had 849 households and 1,324 individuals affected who struggled to cope with the flooding. In Bauchi, Kafin Romi in Gamawa LGA faced extensive damages with 307 households and 1,036 people affected. Miya West in Ganjuwa LGA also felt the with 47 households and 276 individuals. In Borno, Monguno LGA was heavily affected as well. The town of Monguno saw 315 households and 1,146 individuals displaced by the rising waters, struggling with the widespread damage. Gombe, though less affected than some other states, still experienced flooding in certain areas. In Funakaye LGA, Ashaka/Magaba and Bajoga East faced significant challenges with 90 households and 722 individuals affected.

/reports/nigeria-heavy-rainfall-flash-re.summary: On 06 August 2024, heavy rainfall caused significant damage in several camps within the Dikwa and Kala/Balge local government areas (LGAs) of Borno State, including Fulatari, Ajari/Bulamari and Klaguru camps. The intense rainfall led to the destruction and damage of shelters and personal belongings of many displaced households. In total, 243 shelters were damaged, affecting 2,862 individuals across 600 households. The affected population included 777 women, 553 men, and 1,532 children. Of all the needs identified, shelter, non-food items (NFIs), and food were the most prevalent need in the locations affected.

/reports/nigeria-idp-socio-economic-asse.title: Nigeria — IDP Socio-economic Assessment in Adamawa State (June 2025)
/reports/nigeria-idp-socio-economic-asse.summary: The IDP Socio-Economic Survey conducted in Adamawa State in June 2025 offers critical insights into the living conditions and resilience strategies of internally displaced persons (IDPs) residing in camps and camp-like settings. Covering 376 households across 20 sites in four LGAs, the survey was implemented by the Adamawa State Government in collaboration with key partners and supported by the Internal Displacement Solutions Fund (IDSF). About 76 per cent of respondents were displaced before 2016, with many experiencing multiple displacements. In terms of living conditions, 59 per cent of households reported poor or very poor living conditions; only 7 per cent rated their conditions as good. A look into the livelihood assessment showed that agriculture remains the primary source of income, though dependency on humanitarian aid and informal trades has increased. Most households earn less than ₦20,000 monthly. Primary education was the most attained level, representing 54 per cent of respondents. Major barriers to further educational advancement included the cost of school fees, insufficient learning materials, and a shortage of qualified teachers. Despite meeting some of the food security indicators, the survey brought to light that half of the households eat only two meals per day. The reported coping strategies included reducing meal sizes (49%) and skipping meals (42%). Among the 376 households surveyed, 75 per cent reported relying on government hospitals to access health

Covering 376 households across 20 sites in four LGAs, the survey was implemented by the Adamawa State Government in collaboration with key partners and supported by the Internal Displacement Solutions Fund (IDSF). About 76 per cent of respondents were displaced before 2016, with many experiencing multiple displacements. In terms of living conditions, 59 per cent of households reported poor or very poor living conditions; only 7 per cent rated their conditions as good. A look into the livelihood assessment showed that agriculture remains the primary source of income, though dependency on humanitarian aid and informal trades has increased. Most households earn less than ₦20,000 monthly. Primary education was the most attained level, representing 54 per cent of respondents. Major barriers to further educational advancement included the cost of school fees, insufficient learning materials, and a shortage of qualified teachers. Despite meeting some of the food security indicators, the survey brought to light that half of the households eat only two meals per day. The reported coping strategies included reducing meal sizes (49%) and skipping meals (42%). Among the 376 households surveyed, 75 per cent reported relying on government hospitals to access health services and facilities, with limited spending capacity and some reliance on traditional healers or self-medication. The survey highlights the need for flexible, evidence-based, and inclusive approaches to durable solutions, emphasizing the importance of security, livelihoods, and access to services in shaping IDPs’ decisions. Among the 376 households surveyed, 75 per cent reported relying on government hospitals to access health services and facilities, with limited spending capacity and some reliance on traditional healers or self-medication. The survey highlights the need for flexible, evidence-based, and inclusive approaches to durable solutions, emphasizing the importance of security, livelihoods, and access to services in shaping IDPs’ decisions. In response to the evolving humanitarian and recovery needs of internally displaced persons (IDPs), the Adamawa State Government— through the Ministry of Reconstruction, Rehabilitation and Resettlement (MRRR), the State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), and other key ministries and agencies—has prioritized the generation of evidence-based data to inform durable solutions. As part of this effort, a comprehensive Socio-Economic Survey was conducted across IDP camps and camp-like settings in the state. This survey was implemented in collaboration with the State Bureau of Statistics (SBS), the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons (NCFRMI), and supported by the Internal Displacement Solutions Fund (IDSF). The survey aimed to assess the socio-economic conditions of displaced households, including their access to basic services, livelihoods, education, health, shelter and humanitarian assistance. A total of 376 households were interviewed using structured, face-to-face questionnaires administered by trained enumerators. The data collected provide a robust foundation for understanding the living standards, vulnerabilities and resilience capacities of IDPs, and support the design of targeted interventions that promote recovery, inclusion and long-term development. This socio-economic profiling exercise reflects the government’s commitment to ensuring that the needs and aspirations of displaced populations are central to policy and programmatic responses. It also reinforces the importance of localized data in shaping durable solutions that are safe, voluntary and dignified. OBJECTIVES The primary objectives of the socio-economic survey are to: I. Assess the living conditions of IDP households in camps and camp-like settings, including access to shelter, food, water, sanitation, and healthcare. II. Evaluate access to education, livelihoods, and income-generating opportunities among displaced populations. III. Identify gaps in humanitarian assistance and service delivery across sectors. IV. Understand household-level coping mechanisms and resilience strategies in displacement settings. V. Support evidence-based decision-making for recovery, reintegration, and durable solutions programming. METHODOLOGY A structured, face-to-face interview methodology was chosen for the survey to allow for in-depth responses and to account for literacy levels. Interviews were conducted by trained enumerators who administered the survey instrument to each sampled head of household across 20 camps and camp-like settings in Adamawa State. Given the population size of IDPs living in camps and camp-like settings in Adamawa State, the survey targeted a sample of households. This approach ensured representative coverage and maximized data accuracy for analyzing household living conditions. The questionnaire was developed to capture demographic information, household size, length of stay in the camp, and specific living conditions of IDPs living in camps and camp-like settings. Additional questions were included to understand factors influencing these choices, such as safety, access to basic services, livelihood opportunities, and family considerations. The questionnaire was pre-tested in a pilot camp within Adamawa State to ensure clarity, cultural relevance, and suitability. Feedback from the pilot was used to refine the question wording and response options. A team of enumerators fluent in English and local languages (Fulfude, Hausa and Kanuri), as well as familiar with the cultural context of the camps from SEMA and other partners, was trained. The training covered survey objectives, interview techniques, ethical considerations, and the importance of neutrality and confidentiality. Enumerators visited the sampled households within the camps and conducted interviews with the heads of household. In cases where the head was unavailable, a senior household member was interviewed. Responses were recorded digitally on tablets to ensure accuracy and facilitate real-time data entry. Informed consent was obtained from each respondent before beginning the interview. Participants were assured of confidentiality, and responses were anonymized to protect identities. Participation was entirely voluntary, with no repercussions for opting out. Data collected was cleaned, anonymized, and processed for analysis. INTRODUCTION

/reports/nigeria-idp-socio-economic-asse.summary: The IDP Socio-Economic Survey conducted in Borno State provides critical insights into the socio-economic conditions of displaced households, including their access to basic services, livelihoods, education, health, shelter, and humanitarian assistance.
/reports/nigeria-idp-socio-economic-asse.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, AllUsersInDTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Jun 01 2025 Jun 30 2025 Activity Survey Community Perception The IDP Socio-Economic Survey conducted in Borno State provides critical insights into the socio-economic conditions of displaced households, including their access to basic services, livelihoods, education, health, shelter, and humanitarian assistance. Most internally displaced persons (IDPs) surveyed in Borno State experienced multiple displacements, reflecting the protracted nature of the crisis. While 37 per cent of respondents were displaced once, a notable 36 per cent reported being displaced three times, and 4 per cent others experienced four displacements or more. The timing of displacement also illustrates prolonged instability, with only 14 per cent displaced before 2016, while a significant 34 per cent were displaced in 2022, particularly in Mafa, where 59 per cent of displacements occurred that year. This demonstrates a persistent vulnerability to displacement due to ongoing conflict and insecurity in certain areas. Despite prolonged displacement, only 31 per cent of IDP households reported receiving any form of assistance, indicating substantial gaps in aid delivery across affected LGAs. Assistance coverage was lowest in Magumeri (8%) and highest in Dikwa (54%). Living conditions across camps further underscore these vulnerabilities, with 70 per cent of households reporting poor conditions, and 23 per cent rated their situation as very poor. In LGAs such as Mafa and Konduga, nearly all respondents described their conditions as poor or worse, signaling a critical need for improved shelter, services, and infrastructure. The findings highlight the urgent need for targeted and equitable humanitarian interventions. With limited assistance and poor living conditions prevailing in most sites, response strategies must prioritize the most underserved locations. Furthermore, the continued displacement in recent years and high rate of multiple movements in recent years calls for more sustainable, resilience-based programming that addresses the root causes of displacement while enhancing access to basic services, livelihood opportunities, and social protection systems in both camps and host communities. Understand household-level coping mechanisms and resilience strategies in displacement settings. V. Support evidence-based decision-making for recovery, reintegration, and durable solutions programming. METHODOLOGY A structured, face-to-face interview methodology was chosen for the survey to allow for in-depth responses and to account for literacy levels. Interviews were conducted by trained enumerators who administered the survey instrument to each sampled head of household across the camps in Yobe State. Given the population size of IDPs living in camps and camp-like settings in Yobe State, the survey targeted a sample of households. This approach ensured representative coverage and maximized data accuracy for analysing household living conditions. The questionnaire was developed to capture demographic information, household size, length of stay in the camp, and specific living conditions of IDPs living in camps and camp-like settings. Additional questions were included to understand factors influencing these choices, such as safety, access to basic services, livelihood opportunities, and family considerations. The questionnaire was pre-tested in a pilot to ensure clarity, cultural relevance, and suitability. Feedback from the pilot was used to refine question wording and response options. A team of enumerators fluent in English and local languages (Fulfude, Hausa, Kanuri, e.t.c.), as well as familiar with the cultural context of the camps from SEMA and other partners, was trained. The training covered survey objectives, interview techniques, ethical considerations, and the importance of neutrality and confidentiality. Household Interviews: Enumerators visited each household within the camps and conducted interviews with the heads of household. In cases where the head was unavailable, a senior household member was interviewed. Responses were recorded digitally on tablets to ensure accuracy and facilitate real-time data entry. Informed consent was obtained from each respondent before beginning the interview. Participants were assured of confidentiality, and responses were anonymized to protect identities. Participation was entirely voluntary, with no repercussions for opting out. Data collected was cleaned, anonymized, and processed for analysis. INTRODUCTION

In recent years, climate and environmental changes have increasingly affected v arious regions across Nigeria, leading to significant disruptions in the lives of internally displaced persons (IDPs). This report presents an assessment conducted to evaluate the impact of these changes on IDP households living in camps across 10 states in two regions: north-central (Benue, Plateau, Nasarawa, Niger, and Kogi states) and north-west (Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Sokoto, and Zamfara states). The assessment aimed to understand how climate and enviro nmental events such as floods, sandstorms, windstorms, droughts, and erratic rainfall patterns have influenced the livelihoods, migration patterns, and resource access of IDP households. The findings provide valuable insights into the c hallenges faced by IDP households due to climate and environmental changes. The data collected highlights the prevalence of various climate events and their effects on household’s access to resources and overall livelihood. Additionally, the report explores the coping mechanisms employed by these households and the resultant tensions and conflicts arising from increased competition for resources. This assessment is significant because it can inform policymakers, humanitarian agencies, and stakeholders about the pressing needs of IDP households in the context of climate change, environmental degradation and disasters. By understanding the specific impacts and vulnerabilities, targeted interventions can be developed to mitigate the adverse effects and enhance the resilience of these communities. This report is structured to provide a comprehensive analysis of the data collected, presenting findings in percentages to ensure clarity and precision. The subsequent sections detail the methodology, sample size, limitations, survey findings, and conclusions drawn from the assessment. Sample size per state 3.0 LIMITATIONS While the assessment provides valuable insights, several limitations should be noted. First, the sample size in some states, such as Kaduna, could have been larger, which might have limited the generalization of the findings for those states. Efforts were made to ensure proportional representation, but logistical challenges in accessing certain areas may have affected the sample distribution. Secondly, the reliance on self-reported data may introduce response biases, as households might underreport or overreport specific impacts due to recall issues or social desirability. However, trained enumerators and structured questionnaires aimed to minimize these biases and ensure data accuracy. 2.0 METHODOLOGY The assessment emp loyed an approach to gat her quantitative and qu alitative data from IDP households in the targeted regions. A structured questionnai re was designed to capture detailed information on household demographics, clima te event impacts, migration pattern s, resource access, and coping mechanism s. The questionnaire was administered through face-to-face interviews with household heads or representatives. The survey was conduct ed between 22 May 2024 and 02 Jun e 2 024 across 123 camps spread across 10 sta tes, with data collectio n t eams deployed in each state to ensure compreh ensive coverage. En umerators were traine d on the survey tools and data collection t echniques to maintain co nsistency and reliability in the data gathered. The survey included both closed-ended and open -ended questions, allowing household representat ives to provide specific quantitative data and elaborate on their experiences. Data collected were analyzed to generate descriptive statistics, inc luding means, percentages, and frequencies. The analysis focused on understanding the d istribution of responses across different IDP group s in camps and reg ions, highlighting significant patterns and trends. Qualitative data were thematically analyzed t o com plement the quantitative findings a nd p rovide d eeper i nsights i nto t he e xperiences o f I DP households. Quality control measures were imp lemented throughout t he data collection and analysis process. Supervisors conducted regular checks to ens ure data accuracy and completeness, and any discrepancies identified were addressed promptly. The findings presented in this report are based on the aggregated data from all 10 states, ensuring a comprehensive overview of the impact of clim ate and environmental ch anges on 2.1. A survey of 2,306 households was conducted, with the sample size allocated to each state based on the number of IDPs in camps. The median age of household representatives was 50 years. This demographic information is crucial for understanding the perspectives of household heads who are often the primary decision-makers. 5.3 Household demography The demographic composition of households showed that children (0-17 years) made up a significant proportion of the population, with males representing 24 per cent and females 24 per cent, Adults aged (18-59 years) accounted for a substantial part of the population, with males at 22 per cent and females at 25 per cent, while the Elderly aged (60+ years) accounted for a small part of the population with three per cent male and two per cent female. 5.4 Common climate events Households in camp across north-west and north-central reported experiencing various climate and environmental events, with floods at 74 per cent, windstorms at 43 per cent, droughts at 27 per cent, and erratic rainfall patterns at 18 per cent being the most common. /reports/nigeria-ioms-dtm-celebrates-10-.title: Nigeria — IOM's DTM Celebrates 10 years of Excellence in Nigeria
/reports/nigeria-ioms-dtm-celebrates-10-.summary: The IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) was conceptualized in 2004 in Iraq with essential data on displacement to inform humanitarian interventions. Since then, it has been adapted for more than 80 countries, including conflict, climatic shocks, complex emergencies, and prolonged crises. The DTM methodological framework centres on four major components: mobility tracking, flow monitoring, registration, and surveys. The methodology analyses data to disseminate critical multi-layered information on the mobility, vulnerabilities, and needs of displaced and mobile populations, enabling decision-makers and responders to provide better context-specific assistance.
/reports/nigeria-ioms-dtm-celebrates-10-.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact iomnigeriadtm@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Jul 09 2014 Dec 09 2024 Activity Other The IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) was conceptualized in 2004 in Iraq with essential data on displacement to inform humanitarian interventions. Since then, it has been adapted for more than 80 countries, including conflict, climatic shocks, complex emergencies, and prolonged crises. The DTM methodological framework centres on four major components: mobility tracking, flow monitoring, registration, and surveys. The methodology analyses data to disseminate critical multi-layered information on the mobility, vulnerabilities, and needs of displaced and mobile populations, enabling decision-makers and responders to provide better context-specific assistance. In Nigeria, the DTM was established in 2014, covering six states in the north-east (NE): Borno, Adamawa, Yobe, Bauchi, Gombe, and Taraba. In July 2019, DTM expanded to an additional eight states in north-central (NC): Nasarawa, Benue, and Plateau, and north-west (NW): Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Sokoto, and Zamfara, and in 2024 Niger state in the NW and Kogi State in NC were added making a total of 16 states. As of November 2024, DTM Nigeria has access to 107 Local Government Areas (LGAs), 789 wards in the six NE states, and 187 LGAs, 871 Wards in 10 NW and NC states. Cite as

/reports/nigeria-joint-flood-situation-r.title: Nigeria — Joint Flood Situation Report — Adamawa State (2–3 August 2025)
/reports/nigeria-joint-flood-situation-r.summary: The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria.
/reports/nigeria-joint-flood-situation-r.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, AllUsersInDTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Aug 02 2025 Aug 03 2025 Activity Mobility Tracking Event Tracking The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. On 2 and 3 August 2025, the International Organization for Migration (IOM)’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in close coordination and collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) Zonal Office, the Adamawa State Emergency Management Agency (ADSEMA), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the International Rescue Committee (IRC), the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), the World Health Organization (WHO) and 20 other humanitarian partners in Yola South LGA, conducted a Joint Rapid Assessment (JRA) in response to a flash flood incident that occurred overnight across seven communities located across four wards of Bako, Bole Yolde Pate, Makama A and Makama B of Yola South local government area (LGA), Adamawa State. The assessment aimed to understand the extent of the flood’s impact on the affected population and infrastructure and to inform government and humanitarian partners on urgent needs, vulnerabilities, and displacement dynamics. The joint assessment identified a total of 15,128 individuals (or 3,057 households) who were affected by the flood. Of these, 4,890 individuals (or 720 households) were displaced within the host community, while 7,148 individuals (1,853 households) remained in their community despite being significantly impacted. Shelter damage was widespread: 16 per cent of the affected houses were completely destroyed, 38 per cent were partially damaged, and 46 per cent remained habitable but required repairs. The flood also disrupted livelihoods, with over 158 farmlands submerged, posing a long-term threat to food security and income sources, particularly as in 72 per cent of the assessed location, scrop and vegetable farming remains the primary source of income for most residents in the affected areas. Cite as

pdf_text.text: NIGERIA JOINT FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — ADAMAWA STATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.intdtm.iom.int/nigeria For further information, please contact DTM Nigeria DATE OF DATA COLLECTION: 2 and 3 AUGUST 2025 DATE OF PUBLICATION: 19 AUGUST 2025 OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. On 2 and 3 August 2025, the International Organization for Migration (IOM)’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in close coordination and collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) Zonal Office, the Adamawa State Emergency Management Agency (ADSEMA), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the International Rescue Committee (IRC), the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), the World Health Organization (WHO) and 20 other humanitarian partners in Yola South LGA, conducted a Joint Rapid Assessment (JRA) in response to a flash flood incident that occurred overnight across seven communities located across four wards of Bako, Bole Yolde Pate, Makama A and Makama B of Yola South local government area (LGA), Adamawa State. The assessment aimed to understand the extent of the flood’s impact on the affected population and infrastructure and to inform government and humanitarian partners on urgent needs, vulnerabilities, and displacement dynamics. The joint assessment identified a total of 15,128 individuals (or 3,057 households) who were affected by the flood. Of these, 4,890 individuals (or 720 households) were displaced within the host- community, while 7,148 individuals (1,853 households) remained in their community despite being significantly impacted. Shelter damage was widespread: 16 per cent of the affected houses were completely destroyed, 38 per cent were partially damaged, and 46 per cent remained habitable but required repairs. The flood also disrupted livelihoods, with over 158 farmlands submerged, posing a long-term threat to food security and income sources, particularly as in 72 per cent of the assessed location, scrop and vegetable farming remains the primary source of income for most residents in the affected areas. METHODOLOGY The Joint Flood Assessment by IOM’s DTM, NEMA, ADSEMA, NRCS, UNICEF, UNFPA, IRC, NRC, WHO and 20 other humanitarian partners in Yola South LGA employed direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions aimed at gathering data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrated field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for timely harmonised and reliable data collection. Data was triangulated across multiple sources for reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guided the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 15,128 Flood-affected population 202 House completely damaged 21 Functional health facilities after flooding 4,890 Displaced population 50 Water points completely damaged 865 T oilets/latrines affected 61 Water points partially damaged Figure 1. Key highlights 564 Houses flooded but in good condition 460 Houses partially damaged 7,148 Non-displaced population 158 Number of farmlands affected 290 Casualties (Injured 254| Lives lost 36) JOINT FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — ADAMAWA STATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.int dtm.iom.int/nigeria The demographic analysis of the 15,128 individuals affected by flooding in Yola South LGA reveals a varied distribution across age and gender categories, underscoring the need for targeted, inclusive humanitarian responses. Adults aged 18–59 years constitute the largest segment of the affected population, making up 39 per cent in total (21% female, 18% male). Adolescents aged 13–17 years follow closely, representing 32 per cent of those affected, with females accounting for 17 per cent and males 15 per cent. Children between the ages of 1–5 years comprise 19 per cent of the population (10% female, 9% male), while infants under one year of age represent 6 per cent, evenly split at 3 per cent for both genders. The elderly population aged 60 years and above make up the smallest group at 4 per cent (2% female, 2% male). Overall, females represent a slightly higher proportion of the affected population at 53 per cent, compared to 47 per cent male. These demographic insights highlight the necessity for age and gender sensitive interventions, particularly in addressing the needs of adolescents, young children, and women of reproductive age. The depiction and use of boundaries, geographic names, and related data shown on maps and included in this report are not warranted to be error-free, nor do they imply a judgment on the legal status of any territory or any endorsement or acceptance of such boundaries by IOM. This was followed by Bako ward, which accounted for 2,829 individuals (449 households), making up about 19 per cent of the overall population. Makama ‘A’ ward reported 2,571 affected individuals (550 households), comprising 17 per cent of the total, while Makama ‘B’ ward had the lowest impact, with 1,020 individuals (170 households), representing 7 per cent of all those affected. JOINT FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — ADAWAMA STATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.int dtm.iom.int/nigeria Following the flood incident that impacted over 15,128 individuals across the Bako, Bole Yolde Pate, Makama A, and Makama B wards of Yola South LGA, three priority needs were consistently identified by affected populations: shelter, food, and non-food items (NFIs), each representing a critical 100 per cent of the total assessed needs across all surveyed locations. Shelter was highlighted as the most immediate and urgent concern. Many households were rendered homeless or forced into makeshift and overcrowded spaces due to the complete or partial destruction of their homes. With 202 shelters destroyed and 1,226 others requiring repairs, affected families remain vulnerable to harsh weather conditions and health risks. Providing emergency shelter support is essential to protect lives, restore dignity, and reduce exposure to secondary risks such as disease outbreaks. Food insecurity has also become a major challenge in the aftermath of the flooding. With 158 farmlands submerged, access to regular food supplies has been severely disrupted. Families reported significant loss of food stocks, displacement from farmlands, and difficulty accessing local markets. Immediate food assistance is critical to prevent malnutrition, particularly among children, the elderly, and pregnant or lactating women. In addition, the need for NFIs including bedding, cooking utensils, hygiene kits, and clothing was reported across all assessed wards. Many households lost essential items due to the flood waters, further compounding daily struggles and deepening their vulnerability. Timely provision of NFIs will help restore basic living conditions and support the dignity and wellbeing of affected populations. The unanimous prioritization of shelter, food, and NFIs across all affected wards signals the need for a coordinated, multi-sectoral response. Addressing these urgent needs promptly will not only mitigate immediate suffering but also lay the groundwork for longer-term recovery and resilience in flood-affected communities. Many states have been impacted by this year's hefty rains, between August and September, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. These floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have also exacerbated the situation, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. On 27 September 2025, the International Organization for Migration (IOM)’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in close coordination and collaboration with the Kogi State Emergency Management Agency (KOSEMA), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), the Kogi State Ministry of Health, the Kogi State Ministry of Transport, the State Coordinator National Hydroelectric Power Producing Areas Development Commission, Kogi State Fire Service, the National Inland Waterways Authority and the State Universal Basic Education Board, conducted a Joint Rapid Assessment (JRA) in response to flash flooding incident that affected a community in the wards of Oworo in Lokoja LGA. The assessment aimed to understand the extent of the flood’s impact on the affected population and infrastructure and to inform government and humanitarian partners on urgent needs, vulnerabilities, and displacement dynamics. The joint assessment identified 960 individuals (or 160 households) who were affected by the flood. Of these, 576 individuals (96 households) were displaced, while 384 individuals (64 households) remained within their communities as non-displaced. Approximately, 31 per cent of the affected houses were completely destroyed, 28 per cent were partially damaged, and 41 per cent remained habitable but required repairs. The flood also disrupted livelihoods, with farmland measuring up to 10 hectares submerged, posing a long-term threat to food security and income sources. METHODOLOGY The Joint Flood Assessment by IOM’s DTM, KOSEMA, NRCS and six other government agencies in Lokoja LGA employed direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions aimed at gathering data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrated field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for timely harmonized and reliable data collection. Data was triangulated across multiple sources while ethical principles and cultural awareness of local sensitivities guided the process. These findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 960 Flood-affected population 27 House completely destoryed 1 Functional health facility after flooding 576 Displaced population 3 T oilets/latrines affected Figure 1. Adults aged 18–59 years constitute the largest proportion of the affected population, accounting for 48 per cent overall, with females at 25 per cent and males at 23 per cent. Adolescents aged 6–17 years follow, representing 29 per cent of those affected—15 per cent female and 14 per cent male. Children between the ages of 1–5 years comprise 13 per cent of the population, with 7 per cent female and 6 per cent male. The elderly population aged 60 years and above make up 7 per cent, including 4 per cent female and 3 per cent male. At the lower end of the distribution, infants under one year of age represent three per cent of the affected population, split between 2 per cent female and 1 per cent male. Overall, females represent a slightly higher proportion of the affected population at 51 per cent (493 individuals), compared to 49 per cent males (467 individuals). These demographic insights highlight the necessity for age- and gender-sensitive interventions, particularly in addressing the needs of adults, adolescents, and women. /reports/nigeria-joint-intention-survey-.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Jul 21 2025 Jul 25 2025 Activity Survey Return Intention Benue State has experienced recurrent violence in recent years, particularly in rural areas where communities remain vulnerable to attacks and displacement. These incidents have disrupted lives and livelihoods, strained local coping mechanisms, and increased the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) across the state. On 13 and 14 June 2025, Yelwata community in Guma local government area (LGA) was attacked, resulting in loss of lives, destruction of property, and the displacement of thousands of residents. Survivors fled their homes, with many seeking refuge at the International Market IDPs Camp. While some arrived spontaneously, the government facilitated a formal relocation of affected persons. To support joint efforts toward durable solutions and safe, voluntary returns, IOM-DTM Nigeria, in collaboration with the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA) and key partners, conducted a Joint Intention Survey in the International Market IDPs Camp from 21 to 25 July 2025. This initiative was made possible through the combined efforts of the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA), the Benue State Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the Benue State Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agency (BERWASSA), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Catholic Caritas Foundation of Nigeria (CCFN), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS) and the Jireh Doo Foundation (JDF). The collaboration underscores a unified commitment to building resilient communities and addressing the challenges faced by displaced populations. The survey captures the return intentions and priorities of displaced households, providing insight into their current needs, challenges, and aspirations. pdf_text.text: JOINT INTENTION SURVEY ─ BENUE STATE INTERNATIONAL MARKET IDPS CAMP ─ AUGUST 2025 Photo: Yelwata, Benue State © IOM 2025 / Elijah ELAIGWU 2,065 Interviewed HH 3 Average HH Size 38 Average Age of Respondents 14% Male Respondents 86% Female Respondents 9% Men 64% Children KEY FINDINGS 27% Women OVERVIEW Benue State has experienced recurrent violence in recent years, particularly in rural areas where communities remain vulnerable to attacks and displacement. These incidents have disrupted lives and livelihoods, strained local coping mechanisms, and increased the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) across the state. On 13 and 14 June 2025, Yelwata community in Guma local government area (LGA) was attacked, resulting in loss of lives, destruction of property, and the displacement of thousands of residents. Survivors fled their homes, with many seeking refuge at the International Market IDPs Camp. While some arrived spontaneously, the government facilitated a formal relocation of affected persons. To support joint efforts toward durable solutions and safe, voluntary returns, IOM-DTM Nigeria, in collaboration with the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA) and key partners, conducted a Joint Intention Survey in the International Market IDPs Camp from 21 to 25 July 2025. This initiative was made possible through the combined efforts of the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA), the Benue State Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the Benue State Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agency (BERWASSA), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Catholic Caritas Foundation of Nigeria (CCFN), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS) and the Jireh Doo Foundation (JDF). The collaboration underscores a unified commitment to building resilient communities and addressing the challenges faced by displaced populations. The survey captures the return intentions and priorities of displaced households, providing insight into their current needs, challenges, and aspirations. These findings offer a basis for designing targeted interventions that are informed by the lived realities of the affected population and aimed at supporting their return and recovery. METHODOLOGY The primary objective of this survey was to understand the return intentions of households residing in the International Market IDPs Camp, specifically, their willingness and readiness to return to their place of origin, following the attack. A structured, face-to-face interview approach was adopted to allow for meaningful engagement and accommodate varying literacy levels among respondents. Enumerators visited each household in the camp and conducted interviews with the head of household. Where the head was unavailable, another senior household member was interviewed on their behalf. Responses were recorded digitally using tablets to ensure data accuracy and enable real-time entry and validation. Drawing on the population demography from the most recent joint registration exercise conducted at the camp, the baseline population stood at 2,336 households (5,294 individuals). A total of 2,065 households were successfully interviewed, representing a 99 per cent confidence level and a 1 per cent margin of error. This sample provides statistically significant and representative insights into the wider camp population. The survey tool was designed to collect information on household demographics, displacement history, and future intentions. It also explored factors influencing decisions to return or remain displaced, including safety, access to basic services, livelihoods, housing, and family ties. Ethical standards were upheld throughout the exercise. Participation was voluntary, informed consent was obtained from all respondents, and confidentiality was assured. Field supervisors conducted regular spot checks and reviewed submitted data daily to ensure quality control. Upon completion of data collection, responses were cleaned, analyzed, and shared with the Benue State Government and relevant partners to support policy formulation and programmatic planning. 1 JOINT INTENTION SURVEY ─ BENUE STATE INTERNATIONAL MARKET IDPS CAMP ─ AUGUST 2025 DISPLACEMENT HISTORY Findings from the Joint Intention Survey conducted at the International Market IDPs Camp showed that 90 per cent of households have experienced multiple displacements, while 10 per cent have been displaced only once. Among those displaced multiple times, 37 per cent have been displaced more than four times, 24 per cent four times, 20 per cent three times, and 9 per cent twice. This reflects the protracted and cyclical nature of displacement in Benue State, where recurrent violence continues to undermine community stability. Notably, 94 per cent of surveyed households reported that they were last displaced in 2025, a figure that aligns with the violent attack on Yelwata community in June 2025. This incident triggered a large-scale displacement of affected populations to the International Market IDPs Camp and underscores the urgent need for coordinated humanitarian assistance and the implementation of durable solutions to address both the immediate and long-term needs of affected households. INTENTION TO RETURN The survey on return intentions among camp residents offers valuable insights into the future aspirations of IDPs. Approximately 87 per cent of respondents expressed a strong desire to return to their place of origin, highlighting the enduring bond between displaced persons and their ancestral communities. This preference indicates that, despite the recent displacement and emerging challenges, most residents still consider their original homes as the most meaningful and ideal destination for resettlement. Conversely, 13 per cent of respondents indicated no intention to return. This group cited concerns such as insecurity, lack of basic services, and unresolved communal tensions as major deterrents. Their responses point to the need for targeted interventions that address these underlying challenges to ensure that any future return is both voluntary and sustainable. Among respondents who chose to return, 90 per cent indicated a preference to return with their entire household, highlighting the importance of family unity. Six per cent stated they would return alone, while four per cent noted they would not return with their family. 2 JOINT INTENTION SURVEY ─ BENUE STATE INTERNATIONAL MARKET IDPS CAMP ─ AUGUST 2025 10% 90% No Yes Fig 1: Multiple displacements 37% 24% 20% 10% 9% More than 4 times 4 times 3 times Once Twice Fig 2: Number of displacements 1% 2% 1% 1% <1% 94% Before 2016 2016 - 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Fig 3: Year of last displacement 13% 87% No Yes 90% 6% 4% We would return together I will return alone We would not return together Fig 4: Household return intention Fig 5: Planned phases of return REASONS FOR INTENDED RETURN Among respondents intending to return, the leading motivation was the search for livelihood opportunities, reported by 58 per cent of households. This reflects a strong desire for economic stability and self-reliance. Limited employment options at their current location served as a push factor for 45 per cent of respondents, reinforcing the urgency to seek better prospects. Additionally, family reunification was cited by 32 per cent, highlighting the emotional and social bonds that continue to influence return intentions, while 27 per cent expressed a desire to reclaim assets and properties. Other reasons included family ties (21%), improved security at the place of origin (20%), reconstruction needs (19%), and prospects for economic recovery (14%). REASONS FOR NOT RETURNING TO PLACE OF ORIGIN Among respondents who do not intend to return, several key conditions were identified that would need to be addressed before they could consider going back to their communities. The most cited reason was the absence of housing—either destroyed, damaged, or unavailable, reported by 77 per cent of households. Without a place to return to, many families remain unable to envision resettling in their area of origin. The fear of persecution or violence, was the second most prevalent barrier, mentioned by 65 per cent. Trauma and psychosocial distress from previous attacks, as well as the perception of ongoing threats, were highlighted by 58 per cent. Insecurity and the inaccessibility of return areas were cited by 48 per cent as critical concerns. Additionally, 23 per cent reported lacking the financial means to support their return journey, while 21 per cent noted that theft or loss of belongings during displacement presented a significant barrier to returning. HOUSING AVAILABLE/ACCESSIBLE AT INTENDED RETURN LOCATION Of the respondents who intend to return, 69 per cent reported having confirmation that housing was available or accessible at their place of origin. (30 November 2024) OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 28 October and 8 November 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the respective State Emergency Management Agencies (SEMAs), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 1,078 locations in Adamawa, Anambra, Bayelsa, Cross River, Delta, Ebonyi, Edo, Enugu, Imo, Jigawa, Kebbi, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa, Niger, Oyo, Rivers and Taraba states that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessments were jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the 18 states, 191 local government areas (LGAs) and 614 wards that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 2,991,406 individuals in 514,289 households affected by the floods. These individuals included IDPs displaced by the floods and residents impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The total affected population included 896,268 displaced individuals, 153,805 returnees and 1,941,333 non-displaced individuals. METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sources to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Key highlights OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant fl ooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced fac tors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 28 October and 8 November 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Adamawa State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 237 locations in Adamawa State that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, The assessment was jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the humanitarian community on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the 16 local government areas (LGAs) of Adamawa State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 361,919 individuals in 66,360 households affected by the floods. These individuals included IDPs who were displaced by the floods and residents who were impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The affected population included 68,576 displaced individuals in 11,376 households. Fifty-two per cent (52%) of the affected houses were habitable and needed no repair, eighteen per cent were habitable but needed repairs, sixteen per cent were partially damaged and three per cent were totally destroyed. In 70 per cent of the locations assessed, crop farming was among the primary sources of income. METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sour ces to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inf orm emergency response strategies. Children aged 6-17 years account for 27 per cent of the population, with a higher percentage of females 15 per cent compared to males 12 per cent, while the youngest group under 5 years make up 13 per cent, with females (7%) slightly outnumbering males (6%). Elderly individuals aged 60 and above represent 6 per cent, equally distributed between genders. Overall, women are disproportionately affected, constituting 56 per cent of the flood-affected population, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions to address the vulnerabilities of women, children, and the elderly in disaster relief efforts. This indicates a significant strain on local food systems, likely exacerbated by the impacts of flooding, which disrupted livelihoods and left many without reliable access to meals. Immediate food assistance is crucial to mitigate the risk of hunger and malnutrition in these vulnerable populations. Closely following the need for food, in 82 per cent of the locations, key informants identified Non- Food Items (NFIs) as a top priority. (31 December 2024) OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. Furthermore, on 9 September 2024, Maiduguri was affected by a massive flood due to the collapse of Alau dam in the neighbouring Konduga LGA of Borno State. The collapse of the dam exacerbated the flooding in Maiduguri in addition to the continuous heavy rainfall. This marks the first time the Alau Dam has overflowed since 2012. The floods caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 2 and 17 December 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Borno State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 130 locations in Borno State that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessments were jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the 17 local government areas (LGAs), 48 wards and 130 locations that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 1,021,876 individuals in 193,613 households affected by the floods. These individuals included IDPs displaced by the floods and residents impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The total affected population included 121,169 displaced individuals, 756,765 returnees and 143,942 non-displaced individuals. METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sources to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 1,021,876 Flood-affected population 21,791 House completely damaged 190 No shelter 82,939 Houses partially damaged 148 Functional health facility after flooding 2,747 Casualties (Injuries 2,592 | Lives lost 155) 121,169 Displaced population 173 Water points completely damaged 94,245 T oilets/latrines affected 193 Water points partially damaged 756,765 Return population 8,071 Number of farmlands affected 123 Missing persons Fig. 1: Key highlights JOINT POST–FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — BORNO STATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.int dtm.iom.int/nigeria Among school-aged children and adolescents (6-17 years), 16 per cent are female and 13 per cent are male, accounting for 29 per cent of the affected population, with significant implications for disrupted education and development. Children under 5 years (<1 year and 1-5 years) make up 25 per cent of the affected population (4% female, 3% male for infants; 10% female, 8% male for young children), emphasizing their heightened vulnerability and need for targeted support. Adults aged 18-59 years, the working-age population, represent 42 per cent of the affected population (23% female, 19% male). This is the largest single age group impacted, with disruptions to livelihoods posing a challenge to economic recovery. While the elderly (60+ years) comprise only four per cent of the population, they may require specialized care due to age- related vulnerabilities. Food (96%) emerged as the most critical need, this may be due to the destruction of agricultural crops, displacement of communities, and disruptions in food supply chains caused by the flooding. NFIs, prioritized in 73 per cent of locations assessed, encompass essential items such as blankets, clothing, cooking utensils, and hygiene kits. The high demand for NFIs reflected the immediate necessity of restoring basic living conditions for displaced households. Shelter, needed by majority in 65 per cent of the locations, indicating the urgent requirement for safe and adequate housing solutions. Financial assistance was also a significant concern which was identified as a priority need by majority in 40 per cent of the locations assessed, indicating the urgent requirement for cash or voucher support to meet diverse and individualized recovery needs. The loss of livelihoods has compounded the vulnerability of affected households, making these needs pivotal for enabling economic recovery. Cash-based interventions reflect a preference for flexible financial support that allows households to meet varying needs. Health services, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) emerged as secondary needs, each prioritized in 10 per cent and five per cent of the locations respectively. Access to clean water and improved sanitation is essential for preventing disease outbreaks, while healthcare services are critical for addressing flood-related injuries, communicable diseases, and the broader health needs of displaced communities. Education was reported at a much lower level, in three per cent of the locations. Although education disruption due to the floods remains a concern for children and parents, though it is currently overshadowed by more immediate survival needs. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely aﬀecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 28 October and 03 November 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Edo State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA) and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 16 locations in Edo State that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the joint assessment team conducted assessments in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the five local government areas (LGAs) of Edo State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 42,284 individuals in 7,656 households aﬀected by the floods. These individuals included IDPs displaced by the floods and residents impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. Twenty-four per cent (24%) of the aﬀected houses were completely destroyed, 22 per cent were partially damaged and 17 per cent were habitable but need repairs. In 81 per cent of the locations assessed, crop farming was among the primary sources of income.c METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-aﬀ ected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sources to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 6 No shelter JOINT POST-FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — EDO ST ATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.int dtm.iom.int/nigeria The demographic analysis of the population aﬀ ected by the fl ood in Edo State highlights key groups that will require targeted assistance. OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 1 and 6 December 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 10 locations in the FCT that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of 15 key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessment was jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the four local government areas (LGAs) of the Federal Capital T erritory (FCT) that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 3,154 individuals in 507 households affected by the floods. These individuals included IDPs who were displaced by the floods and residents who were impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The affected population included 736 displaced individuals. Forty-four per cent (44%) of the affected houses were habitable but need repair, 27 per cent were habitable and need no repairs, 22 per cent were partially damaged and seven per cent were totally destroyed. In 60 per cent of the locations assessed, crop farming was among the primary sources of income.c METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sources to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 3,154 Flood-affected population 36 House completely damaged None No shelter 333 Houses partially damaged 20 Functional health facility after flooding 6 Casualties (Injuries 2 | lives lost 4) 736 Displaced population 8 Water points completely damaged 71 T oilets/latrines affected 34 Water points partially damaged 1,752 Non-displaced population 589 Number of farmlands affected Fig. 1. Infants and young children are particularly vulnerable to malnutrition, disease, and lack of access to education. These groups require targeted health, nutrition, and educational support. Adults are the largest group of flood-affected individuals, with a higher percentage of females (19%) compared to males (15%). This group includes caregivers and those most directly responsible for rebuilding livelihoods. Assistance in economic recovery and livelihood restoration is crucial for this demographic. The elderly represent a smaller but vulnerable portion of the population, with more females (5%) than males (3%) affected. This group is at greater risk of health complications and mobility challenges, necessitating tailored health and social support services. OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 28 October and 8 November 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Jigawa State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 58 locations in Jigawa State that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of 45 key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessment was jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the 22 local government areas (LGAs) of Jigawa State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 241,046 individuals in 39,779 households affected by the floods. These individuals included IDPs who were displaced by the floods and residents who were impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The affected population included 81,004 displaced individuals. Thirty-two per cent (32%) of the affected houses were completely destroyed, 28 per cent were habitable but need repairs, 24 per cent were partially damaged and 16 per cent were habitable but need repair. In all of the locations assessed, crop farming was the primary source of income.c METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sources to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 241,046 Flood-affected population 12,025 House completely damaged 1,081 No shelter 8,928 Houses partially damaged 102 Functional health facility after flooding 731 Casualties (Injured 616 | Lives lost 115) 81,004 Displaced population 24 Water points completely damaged 10,573 T oilets/latrines affected 33 Water points partially damaged 1 Main source of livelihood 38,048 Number of farmlands affected Fig. 1.
