/reports/nigeria-north-east-jere-lga-bor.title: Nigeria — North-east Jere LGA - Borno State Flash Report (2 March 2024)
/reports/nigeria-north-east-jere-lga-bor.summary: On 2 March 2024, a fire broke out in Muna El-Badawy camp in Jere Local Government Area (LGA) of Borno State. The fire damaged and destroyed the shelters and belongings of numerous displaced households. There was a report of one fatality and no injuries reported. The fire impacted 287 emergency shelters, affecting 1,799 individuals in 257 households. The affected individuals included 1,539 children, 131 women and 129 men. Of all the needs identified, food, shelter and non-food items (NFI) were the most prevalent. Other needs included water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and psychosocial support. As a preventive measure against fire outbreaks, most communities need fire-resistant materials for their shelters and detached shelters.

/reports/nigeria-north-east-konduga-and-.summary: On 06 and 07 February 2024, fires broke out in GSSSS camp Monguno, and Mashamari Kuluye camp of Konduga Local Government Area (LGA) of Borno State, which destroyed the shelters and possessions of many Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs). Many personal items have been lost in the fire, including food items and non-food items. Three fatalities were reported after the incident. The fire destroyed 58 self-made/makeshift shelters affecting 391 individuals in 58 households. The affected individuals included 223 children, 88 women and 80 men.

pdf_text.text: As part of the IDP relocation programme issued by the Borno State Government (BSG), 250 Housing Estate Camp (Dalori II), located in the ward Dalori of Konduga LGA, was closed between 28 July 2022 and 2 August 2022. Following this event, a rapid assessment was conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staﬀ to identify the destinations of the 13,157 IDPs (2,710 households) residing in Dalori II, and to inform the humanitarian community. Following the closure of the camp, many IDPs integrated in host communities in the wards Galitmari (1,648 individuals) and Maimusari (2,395 individuals) in Jere LGA, and the wards Bolori I&II (575 individuals) and Maisandari (1,200 individuals) in M.M.C. LGA. All these host community locations are considered to be part of the urban area of Maiduguri Town. Additionally, an estimated 2,264 IDPs were relocated by the Borno State Government (BSG) to camps and camp-like settings in the ward Buduwa/Bula Chirabe (Banki) and 2,575 individuals to the ward Soye. Both wards are located in Bama LGA of Borno State. The IDPs who arrived in Soye ward integrated with local host communities. Furthermore, 2,500 IDPs integrated in host community locations in Konduga ward of Konduga LGA. /reports/nigeria-north-east-madagali-lga.title: Nigeria — North-east Madagali LGA, Adamawa State Flash Report (27 June 2022)
/reports/nigeria-north-east-madagali-lga.summary: The lingering conflict in Nigeria's North East Zone has been the major cause of widespread population displacement. Over 2 million persons have been forced to leave their areas of residence in search of safety and security in neighbouring wards and LGAs.
/reports/nigeria-north-east-madagali-lga.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, AllUsersInDTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Period Covered Jun 20 2022 Jun 20 2022 Activity Mobility Tracking Event Tracking The lingering conflict in Nigeria's North East Zone has been the major cause of widespread population displacement. Over 2 million persons have been forced to leave their areas of residence in search of safety and security in neighbouring wards and LGAs. On 20 June 2022, a Non-State Armed Group (NSAG) carried out an attack in Madagali ward in Madagali LGA of Adamawa State, leading to a wave of population displacement. Following the attack, a rapid assessment was conducted by DTM field staff with the purpose of informing the humanitarian community and government partners, and enabling targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of the affected population. As a result of the attack, a total of 665 individuals from 133 households were displaced from their communities in Madagali ward to neighbouring localities within the same ward. The majority of those affected are refugees who are initially displaced from Cameroon. The displaced population is currently residing with residents in the host community and are in need of shelter, NFIs and food. Cite as

/reports/nigeria-north-east-maiduguri-me.title: Nigeria — North East — Maiduguri Metropolitan Council LGA (Borno State) Flash Report  (03 December 2021)
/reports/nigeria-north-east-maiduguri-me.summary: As part of the IDP relocation programme issued by the Borno State Government (BSG), the IDPs residing in Bakasi Camp were relocated to their LGAs of origin.
/reports/nigeria-north-east-maiduguri-me.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, AllUsersInDTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Nov 21 2021 Dec 01 2021 Activity Event Tracking Mobility Tracking As part of the IDP relocation programme issued by the Borno State Government (BSG), the IDPs residing in Bakasi Camp were relocated to their LGAs of origin. On 21 November 2021, the Borno State Government (BSG) commenced the relocation of the IDPs residing in Bakasi Camp, located in Maisandari ward in the MMC LGA of Borno State. Following this event, a rapid assessment was conducted by DTM field staff in order to capture these IDP movements, inform the humanitarian community and enable targeted assistance to the BSG. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of the repatriated population. Between 21 November and 01 December, an estimated number of 4,378 individuals or 769 households were relocated from Bakasi Camp to various locations in the state. Parts of the IDP population organised the relocation themselves, others were assisted by the Borno State Government. Of the total IDP movement, 955 individuals or 161 households relocated to camps or camp-like settings in Gwoza LGA, while 2,029 individuals or 347 households were hosted by the local communities of Gwoza LGA. Camps and camp-like settings in Monguno welcomed a total of 889 individuals in 169 households, while 505 individuals in 92 households are currently hosted by communities in Monguno LGA. Cite as

MOBILITY TRACKING — IDP AND RETURNEE ATLAS NIGERIA — NORTH-EAST Round 46 (December 2023) 3 The IDP and returnee atlas is the product of the DTM Master list assessment which gathers data at site/location level using multiple key informants and direct observations. Interviews are conducted face-to-face by DTM in accessible locations. The atlas provides data on the number of IDPs and returnees at the state, local government area, ward and location levels, their shelter type, the period of displacement, areas of origin for IDPs and areas of last displacement for returnees. The Master list presents data on the number of individuals and households using either head count, previous registration, official documentation or a demographic calculator based on a sample of assessed IDPs dispersed in host communities, camps or camp-like settings. METHODOLOGY • Insecurity remains the major hinderance to DTM assessments in the North-east, limitiing the field teams access to some locations with returnees and IDPs. • Transportation of many remote and hard-to-reach areas have become more difficult as a result of inflation in the cost of transportation. • Some enumerators experienced hesitance and reluctance from internally displaced populations to cooperate with the surveys as data is collected regularly and assistance is limited. • The data used for this analysis were estimates obtained through key informant interviews, direct observation and focus group discussions. Thus, to ensure these estimates’ reliability, data collection was performed at the lowest administrative level: the site or the host community. LIMITATIONS MOBILITY TRACKING — IDP AND RETURNEE ATLAS NIGERIA — NORTH-EAST Round 46 (December 2023) This report, which presents the results from Round 46 of Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) assessments carried out by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), aims to improve the understanding of the scope of internal displacement, and return movements and to better understand dynamics and trends of displacement in the conflict-affected region. north-east Nigeria. The assessment for this atlas took place between July and September 2023 and reflects the number of IDPs from the six states in Nigeria’s north-east geopolitical zone. This zone is the most affected by the conflict and consists of the following states: Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Taraba and Yobe. This report also contains findings on returnees from the master list assessment conducted in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states which are the most affected states in the north-east zone. In Round 46, a total of 2,305,335 Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) were identified in 472,239 households. This signifies a slight increase of less than one per cent (or 9,801 individuals) compared to Round 45 when 2,295,534 IDPs were recorded (June 2023). During Round 46, IDP assessments were conducted in 2,333 locations across the six states of north-east Nigeria. The assessed locations included 273 camps and camp-like settlements and 2,060 locations where internally displaced persons lived among host communities. Furthermore, 2,083,835 returnees were recorded in the Round 46 assessment. This number represents an increase of 8,578 individuals or less than one per cent compared to Round 45 when 2,075,257 returnees were recorded in June 2023. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The population categories are defined in this report as follows: • An Internally Displaced Person (IDP) according to DTM definition is ‘a person who has been forced to flee or to leave his or her home or place of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who has not crossed an internationally recognized state border.’ • In the context of Nigeria, a returnee is defined by DTM as any former IDP who returned to his or her locality of origin (IDP returnee); or any former refugee who returned to his or her country of origin (returnee from abroad). MOBILITY TRACKING — IDP AND RETURNEE ATLAS NIGERIA — NORTH-EAST Round 48 (November 2024) 3 MOBILITY TRACKING — IDP AND RETURNEE ATLAS NIGERIA — NORTH-EAST Round 48 (November 2024) This report, which presents the results from Round 48 of Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) assessments carried out by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), aims to improve the understanding of the scope of internal displacement, and return movements and to better understand dynamics and trends of displacement in the conflict-affected region. The assessment for this atlas took place between July and September 2024 and reflects the number of IDPs from the six states in Nigeria’s north-east geopolitical zone. This zone is the most affected by the conflict and consists of the following states: Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Taraba and Yobe. This report also contains findings on returnees from the master list assessment conducted in Borno, Adamawa and Yobe states which are the most affected states in the north-east zone. In Round 48, a total of 2,255,595 internally displaced persons (IDPs) were identified in 465,669 households. This signifies a slight decrease of less than one per cent (or 4,068 individuals) compared to Round 47. During Round 48, IDP assessments were conducted in 2,264 locations across the six states of north-east Nigeria. The assessed locations included 250 camps and camp-like settlements and 2,014 locations where IDPs lived among host communities. Furthermore, 2,110,477 returnees in 348,341 householdswere recorded in the Round 48 assessment. This number represents an increase of 16,873 individuals or one per cent increment compared to Round 47 when 2,093,604 returnees were recorded in June 2024. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The IDP and returnee atlas is the product of the DTM Master list assessment which gathers data at site/location level using multiple key informants and direct observations. Interviews are conducted face-to-face by DTM in accessible locations. The atlas provides data on the number of IDPs and returnees at the state, local government area, ward and location levels, their shelter type, the period of displacement, areas of origin for IDPs and areas of last displacement for returnees. The Master list presents data on the number of individuals and households using either head count, previous registration, official documentation or a demographic calculator based on a sample of assessed IDPs dispersed in host communities, camps or camp-like settings. METHODOLOGY LIMITATIONS • Insecurity remains the major hinderance to DTM assessments in the North-east, limitiing the field teams access to some locations with returnees and IDPs. • Transportation of many remote and hard-to-reach areas have become more difficult as a result of inflation in the cost of transportation. • Some enumerators experienced hesitance and reluctance from internally displaced populations to cooperate with the surveys as data is collected regularly and assistance is limited. • The data used for this analysis were estimates obtained through key informant interviews, direct observation and focus group discussions. Thus, to ensure these estimates’ reliability, data collection was performed at the lowest administrative level: the site or the host community. POPULATION CATEGORY The population categories are defined in this report as follows: • An Internally Displaced Person (IDP) according to DTM definition is ‘a person who has been forced to flee or to leave his or her home or place of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who has not crossed an internationally recognized state border.’ • In the context of Nigeria, a returnee is defined by DTM as any former IDP who returned to his or her locality of origin (IDP returnee); or any former refugee who returned to his or her country of origin (returnee from abroad). MOBILITY TRACKING — IDP AND RETURNEE ATLAS NIGERIA — NORTH-EAST Round 48 (November 2024) IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) provides support to the Government and humanitarian partners by establishing a comprehensive system that collects, analyses and disseminates data on IDPs and returnees to ensure timely and effective assistance to the affected populations. Data collection takes place at a granular level and is repeated at regular intervals to ensure accurate and up-to-date information. As of September 2024, the DTM identified a total of 2,255,595 IDPs in 465,669 households and 2,110,477 returnees in 348,341 households. The IDP population included IDPs in camps and camp-like settings (941,153 individuals or 42%) and IDPs residing in host communities (1,314,442 individuals or 58%). The returnee population included IDP returnees (1,785,752 individuals or 85%) and returnees from abroad (324,725 individuals or 15%). /reports/nigeria-north-east-mobility-tra.summary: In Round 50, 2,292,477 IDPs were identified in 475,234 households and 2,189,318 returnees were identified in 361,953 households. The IDP population included IDPs in camps and camp-like settings (955,135 individuals or 41%), IDPs in host communities (1,234,898 individuals or 54%), and IDPs on a durable solution pathway (102,444 individuals or 5%). The IDPs on the pathway to durable solutions is IDPs relocated (40,887 individuals or 2%) and IDPs integrated (61,557 individuals or 3%). The IDP and returnee population recorded a slight increase of approximately 2 per cent (40,129 individuals) and 3 per cent (59,993 individuals) respectively compared to Round 49 (covering October to November 2024). One of the main reasons for the increase in the IDP population is non-state actors' attacks, followed by other factors such as natural disaster, seasonal mobility due to farming, and the search for safety, security, or better services. The rise in the returnee population is due to improved security in areas of origin. During Round 50, the IDP and returnee assessment was conducted in 3,128 locations across the six north-east states in Nigeria. The assessed locations included 248 camps and camp-like settlements, 1,774 locations where IDPs live among host communities, 64 sites with relocated IDPs, 196 sites with integrated IDPs and 846 return locations (as of April 2025).

International Organization for Migration (IOM), which aims to improve and better understand the dynamics and trend of internal displacement in the north-east of Nigeria, a region particularly affected by conflict. One of the main reasons for the increase in the IDP population is non-state actors attacks, followed by other factors such as natural disaster, seasonal mobility due to farming, and the search for safety, security, or better services. The rise in the returnee population is due to improved security in areas of origin. During Round 50, the IDP and returnee assessment was conducted in 3,128 locations across the six north-east states in Nigeria. The assessed locations included 248 camps and camp-like settlements, 1,774 locations where IDPs live among host communities, 64 sites with relocated IDPs, 196 sites with integrated IDPs and 846 return locations (as of April 2025). The Master list presents data on the number of individuals and households using head count, previous registration, official documentation or a demographic calculator based on a sample of assessed IDPs dispersed in host communities, camps or camp-like settings. METHODOLOGY LIMITATIONS Insecurity remains the major challenge to DTM assessments in the north-east, limiting or preventing access to certain locations. Transportation to many remote and hard-to-reach areas have become more difficult as a result of inflation in the cost of transportation. Some enumerators experienced hesitance and reluctance from internally displaced populations to cooperate with the surveys as data is collected regularly and assistance is limited. The data used for this analysis were estimates obtained through key informant interviews, direct observation and focus group discussions. Thus, to ensure these estimates’ reliability, data collection was performed at the lowest administrative level (site or host community). POPULATION CATEGORY The population categories are defined in this report as follows: • An Internally Displaced Person (IDP) according to DTM, is ‘a person who has been forced to flee or to leave his or her home or place of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who has not crossed an internationally recognized state border.’ • In the context of Nigeria, a returnee is defined by DTM as any former IDP who returned to his or her locality of origin (IDP returnee); or any former refugee who returned to his or her country of origin (returnee from abroad).

/reports/nigeria-north-east-monguno-lga-.title: Nigeria — North-east Monguno LGA - Borno State Flash Report (23 January 2024)
/reports/nigeria-north-east-monguno-lga-.summary: On 22 January 2024, fires broke out in Flutari, Gana Ali, and Water Board camps in Monguno Local Government Area (LGA) of Borno State, which destroyed the shelters and possessions of many Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs). Many personal items were lost in the fire, including food ration cards and biometric identification cards. There were no reported injuries or fatalities. The fire destroyed 73 makeshift shelters affecting 287 individuals in 68 households. The affected individuals included 131 children, 88 women and 68 men. The victims need shelter and shelter repair kits, other needs include food and NFIs (non-food items). No assistance has been rendered to the affected population at the time of reporting.

pdf_text.text: Event Overview On 26 and 27 February 2026, armed bandit attacks occurred in the communities of Mansur, T eshan Dutse, and Gwana in Gwana/Mansur ward of Alkaleri LGA of Bauchi State. According to key informants, the attacks displaced a total of 12,168 individuals from 2,857 households. The displaced population included 4,338 children, 5,030 women, and 2,800 men. In Mansur, 1,350 individuals were displaced to Futuk Primary School in Futuk ward, 600 individuals were displaced to the community of Anguwan Abdullahi Mai Ki/f_i in Yalo ward, 65 individuals were displaced from T eshan Dutse to Yelenguruza in Yalo ward of Alkaleri LGA, Bauchi State, and 10,153 individuals from Gwana /f_led to the Vocational Training Centre in Kashere ward of Akko LGA in Gombe State. Overall, 111 casualties were reported as a result of the attacks, including 104 injuries and seven fatalities. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) /f_ield staﬀ conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, alongside the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response. Food, non-food items (NFIs), water sanitation and hygiene (WASH), shelter, healthcare and transport were the most prevalent needs identi/f_ied. Other needs include security and psychosocial support. The north-east region of Nigeria is grappling with an intricate displacement crisis, exacerbated by both human con/f_lict and environmental factors. Equally, non-state armed groups (NSAGs) perpetuate violence, which often drives large-scale displacement. The escalation of violence in 2014 triggered a multifaceted humanitarian emergency, leading to mass displacement across the area. De/f_inition of terms: Displaced: People who have left the site of the incident (e.g. their home or community), because of the incident (con/f_lict, disaster, violence, etc.), and are now living elsewhere (Internally Displaced Person). Non-displaced: People who remain at the location after the incident, they did not leave, despite being aﬀected. Aﬀected (total): All individuals impacted by the incident, including both those who were displaced and those who stayed (non-displaced). pdf_text.text: Event Overview Between 13 and 14 September 2025, multiple flood incidents were reported across three camps in the local government area (LGA) of Dikwa in Borno State. These incidents affected 5,829 individuals in 1,058 households. This included 3,350 children, 1,364 women, and 1,115 men. The incident affected 895 shelters, 46 shelters were partially damaged and 849 shelters were completely destroyed. The flooded camps included 1000 Camp, Alhaji Bashir Camp and Kamchiji Camp in Dikwa ward of Dikwa LGA. Non-food items (NFIs), shelter and food were the most prevalent needs identified. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, alongside the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response. Nigeria's north-east region is increasingly affected by climate-related disasters, particularly seasonal flooding caused by heavy rainfall and riverbank/dam overflows. The north-east region of Nigeria grapples with a deeply intricate displacement crisis exacerbated by both human conflict and environmental factors. The non-state armed groups (NSAGs) perpetuate violence, driving large-scale displacement. The escalation of violence in 2014 triggered a multifaceted humanitarian emergency, leading to mass displacement across the area. Individuals Aﬀected 5,829 *Multi-select answers allowed Figure. 2. /reports/nigeria-north-east-nigeria-zamf.title: Nigeria — North-east Nigeria — Zamfara State Flash Report 281 (13 March 2026)
/reports/nigeria-north-east-nigeria-zamf.summary: On 12 March 2026, an armed bandit attack occurred in the community of Rafin Marke in Yashi Ward of Bukkuyum Local Government Area (LGA) in Zamfara State. According to key informants, the attack displaced a total of 622 individuals from 110 households. Of these, 270 individuals were displaced to the community of Nasarawa in Nasarawa Ward, while 352 individuals were displaced to the community of Marafan Garangi in Zurummai Ward, all within Bukkuyum LGA. The displaced population included 347 children, 152 women, and 123 men. A total of nine casualties were reported, including seven injuries and two fatalities.

/reports/nigeria-north-east-site-assessm.title: Nigeria — North East — Site Assessment Dashboard 38 (June — July 2021)
/reports/nigeria-north-east-site-assessm.summary: In response to the need for accurate and up-to-date information on human mobility and forced displacement in North East Nigeria, IOM activated its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) to support the Government and the humanitarian community with multi-layered data on the numbers, trends, status, locations and needs of populations affected by the on-going conflict in North East Nigeria. Round 38 of assessment was conducted from 21 June to 27 July 2021.
/reports/nigeria-north-east-site-assessm.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, AllUsersInDTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Jun 21 2021 Jul 27 2021 Activity Mobility Tracking Baseline Assessment In response to the need for accurate and up-to-date information on human mobility and forced displacement in North East Nigeria, IOM activated its Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) to support the Government and the humanitarian community with multi-layered data on the numbers, trends, status, locations and needs of populations affected by the on-going conflict in North East Nigeria. Round 38 of assessment was conducted from 21 June to 27 July 2021. During Round 38, site assessments were conducted in 2,380 locations. Assessed locations included 309 camps and camp-like settlements as well as 2,071 locations where internally displaced persons were living among host communities (down from 2,089 in Round 37). The purpose was to better understand the gaps in services provided and the needs of the affected population. Site assessments included an analysis of sector-wide needs, shelter and non-food items, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), food and nutrition, health, education, livelihood, security, communication and protection. This dashboard presents key findings from these site assessments. DTM identified 879,400 IDPs living in the 309 assessed sites. 81 per cent of IDPs were women and children. 68% of IDPs cited tarpaulin as the most needed shelter material, while 47% of IDPs cited blanket/mat as the most needed NFI. 13% of IDPs do not have access to regular medication, and 21% of IDPs do not have access to food support. In 86% of the sites surveyed, IDPs cited food as the main unmet need. Cite as

/reports/nigeria-north-east-song-lga-ada.title: Nigeria — North-east Song LGA Adamawa State Flash Report (19 July 2022)
/reports/nigeria-north-east-song-lga-ada.summary: With the onset of the rainy season in Nigeria’s northeastern state of Adamawa, varying degrees of damages have been reported in multiple locations in the region. Heavy rainfalls, accompanied by strong winds have caused serious damages to shelters and infrastructures. On 17 July  2022, heavy rainfalls in Song LGA in Adamawa State resulted in the flooding of the Loko communities in the ward Song Gari. IOM’s DTM programme carried out assessments to ascertain the level of damage sustained in the affected communities. Over 1,200 individuals from 148 households were displaced from Song Gari Ward in Song LGA to neighbouring wards in the LGAs Gombi, Girei, Maiha and Yola North also situated in Adamawa State.

On 17 July 2022, heavy rainfalls in Song LGA in Adamawa State resulted in the flooding of the Loko communities in the ward Song Gari. Over 1,200 individuals from 148 households were displaced from Song Gari Ward in Song LGA to neighbouring wards in the LGAs Gombi, Girei, Maiha and Yola North also situated in Adamawa State. An estimated 148 individuals are currently residing in the Secretariat of Song LGA. While others left to stay with relatives in neigbouring LGAs. In total, 100 shelters were either damaged or flooded by storms, leaving a total of 100 households in immediate need of shelter. Four casualties were reported as a result of the storms. /reports/nigeria-north-east-sulumri-baki.title: Nigeria — North-east Sulumri Bakin Kwalta, Maiduguri M.C. LGA — (Borno State) Fire Outbreak Flash Report 29 March 2022
/reports/nigeria-north-east-sulumri-baki.summary: On 27 March 2022, a fire outbreak was reported at Sulumri Bakin Kwalta Camp in Maiduguri M.C. LGA of Borno State. The fire damaged and destroyed shelters and belongings of numerous IDP households. The fire incident fully destroyed 69 emergency shelter, 14 temporary shelters, affecting a total of 482 individuals in 91 households. The affected individuals included 276 children, 115 women and 91 men. Additionally, four goats died in the fire outbreak and other properties were destroyed. A block of shower and toilets were partially damaged by the fire.

pdf_text.text: Event Overview On 17 and 20 May 2025, non-state armed groups (NSAGs) attacked the Hausari community in Mairari Ward and Lawandi community in Bultuwa/Mar/ Yaro Ward of Yunusari local government area (LGA) in Yobe State. The attacks affected 355 individuals from 60 households. Of the total aﬀected individuals, 185 were children, 98 were women, and 72 were men. Fifteen casualties were reported during the incidents: /f_ive fatalities and 10 injuries. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted a rapid assessment and identified shelter, non-food items (NFIs), and food as the most urgent needs of the affected population. Other essential needs included transportation. The findings from this rapid assessment aimed to inform humanitarian actors and government partners to help coordinate an effective and targeted response. The north-east region of Nigeria grapples with a deeply intricate displacement crisis, exacerbated by both human conflict and environmental factors. Non-state armed groups (NSAGs) perpetuate violence, driving large-scale displacement. The escalation of violence in 2014 triggered a multifaceted humanitarian emergency, leading to mass displacement across the area. Individuals Aﬀected 355 *Multiple choices selected Fig. 2. As of May 2025, a total of 1,252,042 IDPs in 216,288 households were identified—representing a five per cent decrease compared to Round 16. /reports/nigeria-north-west-kaduna-state.title: Nigeria — North-west — Kaduna State Flash Report 212 (27 May 2025)
/reports/nigeria-north-west-kaduna-state.summary: On 25 May 2025, a severe windstorm incident occurred in Kaduna State, affecting residents of Angwan Gobarawa community in Buda ward of Kajuru local government area (LGA).
/reports/nigeria-north-west-kaduna-state.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, iomnigeriadtm@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Snapshot Date May 27 2025 Activity Mobility Tracking Event Tracking On 25 May 2025, a severe windstorm incident occurred in Kaduna State, affecting residents of Angwan Gobarawa community in Buda ward of Kajuru local government area (LGA). The windstorm impacted a total of 38 households and 228 individuals, including 108 males and 120 females. Tragically, the incident resulted in two casualties. Additionally, 18 shelters were partially damaged, Residents of the affected community remain within Kajuru LGA, no displacement across LGAs or state boundaries has been observed. However, the situation has significantly disrupted daily life and created an urgent need for humanitarian assistance. Initial needs identified include emergency shelter support, household and non - food items (NFIs), and food assistance. The affected households are currently relying on host communities for support and remain vulnerable to the elements due to the partial shelter damage. Following these events, the DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. /reports/nigeria-north-west-kaduna-state.title: Nigeria — North-west — Kaduna State Flash Report 238 (14 July 2025)
/reports/nigeria-north-west-kaduna-state.summary: Between 10 and 14 July 2025, windstorms and rainfall in Kaduna State affected communities in Giwa, Lare, Makarfi, Soba and Ikara Local Government Areas (LGAs), particularly within: the Yakawada, Giwa, Pan Hauya, and Danmahawayi wards of the Giwa LGA; Saminaka, Abadawa, Lazuru, Lere, Dan Alhaji, Yar Kasuwa, Gure/Kahugu, and Ramin Kura wards of the Lere LGA; Makarfi, Tudun Wada, Gazara, Danguziri, Gimi, Gwanki and Dandamisa wards of the Makarfi LGA; Maigana, Gimba, Soba, Danwata, Rahama, Turawa, Kinkiba and Kwasallo wards of the Soba LGA; Auchan, Rumi, Saulawa, Pala, Ikara, Kuya, Janfala, K/Kogi and Saya-Saya wards of the Ikara LGA. The windstorms and rainfall impacted 6,172 individuals (1,026 households), including 2,710 males and 3,462 females. The incident resulted in six casualties and 864 damaged shelters, affecting the living conditions of all the residents. Residents of the affected communities remain within their respective LGAs, with no displacement to other LGAs or states. The primary needs identified include food, shelter, security, health, and non-food items (NFIs). Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, as well as the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response.

The attacks affected 4,807 individuals across 644 households, displacing 4,510 individuals across 316 households. Among the affected individuals were 3,088 children, 904 women and 815 men, resulting in 28 injuries and 13 fatalities. On 14 and 15 May 2025, a windstorm affected the communities of Yar Gamji in Darini/Magaji/Abu ward of Batsari LGA; Kandawa and Dankar in Kandawa ward of Batsari LGA; Mallamawa in G/Baure/Mallamawa ward of Jibia LGA and Kukar Gesa in Wakilin Gabas I ward of Katsina LGA. The disaster affected 5,690 individuals across 771 hoseholds and displaced 1,412 individuals across 207 households to neighbouring communities in Batsari and Jibia LGAs. The affected individuals included 3,682 children, 1,078 women, and 930 men, resulting in 47 injuries and four fatalities.

/reports/nigeria-north-west-katsina-stat.title: Nigeria — North-west — Katsina State Flash Report 214 (29 May 2025)
/reports/nigeria-north-west-katsina-stat.summary: Between 21 and 23 May 2025, a series of armed attacks were recorded across three local government areas (LGAs) in Katsina State, namely Safana, Dan Musa, and Sabuwa. In Safana LGA, Kukar Samu community in Babban Duhu 'B' ward was attacked, affecting 864 individuals from 128 households. In Dan Musa LGA, Galadima and Rugar Gyada communities in Yan-Tumaki B ward were attacked across two consecutive days, impacting 778 individuals from 110 households. Meanwhile, in Sabuwa LGA, the Tudun Amiru-Burdugau community in Dugun Mu’azu ward was also attacked, affecting 385 individuals from 55 households. These attacks displaced 502 individuals from 66 households who fled the violence to seek safety. Seventeen fatalities were recorded, and 53 others sustained injuries, with extensive damage to 35 shelters. The affected population—comprising 968 men and 1,059 women—urgently needs food, shelter, protection, and medical support. On 22 May 2025, a violent windstorm hit Shimfida community in G/Baure/Mallamawa ward of Jibia LGA. The storm impacted 406 individuals across 57 households, destroying 26 shelters—16 partially and 10 completely. Although no fatalities were recorded, 18 individuals were injured, and affected families remain in urgent need of shelter and relief assistance.

The disaster affected 1,888 individuals across 277 households and displaced 233 individuals across 34 households. The displaced persons relocated to Sabon layi community in Dandume ‘B’ ward within the same LGA. The affected individuals comprised 1,182 children, 377 women and 329 men, resulting in two injuries. Security, food, shelter and non-food items (NFIs) were the most prevalent needs identified. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, alongside the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response.

/reports/nigeria-north-west-nigeria-jiga.summary: Between 21 and 26 September 2025, severe flooding caused by heavy rainfall and river overflows affected five local government areas (LGAs) across Jigawa State, including Guri, Kiri Kasamma, Birniwa, Jahun, and Ringim. The incident led to widespread damage to homes, shelters, and community infrastructure across host communities. Although all affected individuals remain within their communities, with no displacement to other wards or LGAs, others expressed intentions to relocate to safer areas or return to the location of incident once floodwaters recede. The primary needs identified across all the affected wards include shelter, food, health support, and non-food items (NFIs).

pdf_text.text: Event Overview Between 21 and 26 September 2025, severe /f_looding caused by heavy rainfall and river over/f_lows aﬀected /f_ive local government areas (LGA s) across Jigawa State, including Guri, Kiri Kasamma, Birniwa, Jahun, and Ringim. The incident led to widespread damage to homes, shelters, and community infrastructure across host communities. The flooding impacted 5,878 individuals (1,140 households), comprising 2,972 males and 2,906 females. Although all affected individuals remain within their communities, with no displacement to other wards or LGAs, others expressed intentions to relocate to safer areas or return to the location of incident once floodwaters recede. pdf_text.text: Event Overview On 18 January 2026, an armed attack attributed to non-state armed groups (NSAGs) was reported in Kurmin Wali community, Idon Ward of Kajuru LGA, Kaduna State. The incident affected a total of 882 individuals from 146 households, these included 199 children, 295 women, and 388 men. Among the affected individuals, key informants reported that 156 individuals from 25 households were displaced, fleeing mainly to the neighbouring community including Doka Avong and Idon Hanya in Idan ward of Kajuru LGA. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, alongside the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response. Food, shelter, water, security, psychosocial support and non-food items (NFIs) were the most prevalent needs identified. Nigeria’s north-west region has had long-standing tensions between farmers and herders, as well as ethnic and religious groups, which often lead to conflicts, attacks, and banditry or ‘hirabah’. These incidents involve kidnapping and theft along major highways. The crisis has intensified in recent years, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-west region. Definition of terms: Displaced: People who have left the site of the incident (e.g. their home or community), because of the incident (conflict, disaster, violence, etc.), and are now living elsewhere (Internally Displaced Person). Non-displaced: People who remain at the location after the incident, they did not leave, despite being affected. Affected (total): All individuals impacted by the incident, including both those who were displaced and those who stayed (non-displaced). /reports/nigeria-north-west-nigeria-kats.summary: On 31 July and 3 August 2025, armed bandits attacked the communities of Kyambarawa in Shinka ‘B’ ward of Katsina local government area (LGA) and Garin Awala in Sayau ward of Sabuwa LGA in Katsina State. The attacks affected 10,360 individuals across 1,626 households and displaced 5,013 individuals across 788 households. The displaced persons relocated to Modoji Gari community in Shinka ‘A’ ward of Katsina LGA and Unguwar Haruna community in Makera ward of Funtua LGA. The affected individuals comprised 6,652 children, 1,943 women and 1,765 men, resulting in 14 injuries and 8 fatalities.

The attacks affected 10,360 individuals across 1,626 households and displaced 5,013 individuals across 788 households. The displaced persons relocated to Modoji Gari community in Shinka ‘A’ ward of Katsina LGA and Unguwar Haruna community in Makera ward of Funtua LGA. The affected individuals comprised 6,652 children, 1,943 women and 1,765 men, resulting in 14 injuries and 8 fatalities. On 31 July and 8 August 2025, floods affected the communities of Sabuwar Unguwa in Wakili Kudu III ward of Katsina LGA, Tudun Baras in Wakilin Arewa (B) ward of Katsina LGA, Agangaro in Kusa ward of Jibia LGA and Sabon Gari in Danja ‘B’ ward of Danja LGA in Katsina State. The disaster affected 20,826 individuals across 3,213 households and displaced 1,706 individuals across 278 households. /reports/nigeria-north-west-nigeria-kats.summary: On 01 and 06 April 2026, armed bandit attacks occurred in the communities of Yar Dorowa and Gobirawa in Yan-Tumaki B Ward of Dan Musa Local Government Area (LGA) in Katsina State. According to key informants, the attacks affected 693 individuals across 91 households, including 385 children, 169 women, and 139 men. Of the affected population, 485 individuals from 65 households were displaced to the community of Yantumaki in Yan-Tumaki A Ward of Dan Musa LGA. A total of 29 casualties were reported across both incidents, comprising 24 injuries and five fatalities.

pdf_text.text: Event Overview Between 9 and 14 August 2026, armed bandits attacked the communities of Labo Kankia in Kurami Yankwani ward of Bakori Local Government Area (LGA), Magaji Wondo Dansuda in Magaji Wondo ward, Gyazamar and Bokolo in Dandume A ward, Unguwar Rimin Jiruwa in Dandume B ward of Dandume LGA and Daddara in Kusa ward of Jibia LGA, all in Katsina State. According to key informants, the attacks aﬀected 2,723 individuals across 629 households and displaced 1,535 individuals from 218 households, including 697 children, 495 women, and 343 men. Of the displaced population, 1,260 individuals moved from the community of Labo Kankia to the community of Unguwar Malam Tajo in Kurami Yankwani ward of Bakori LGA, 91 individuals moved from Unguwar Rimin Jiruwa to the community of Dogon Kawo in Mahuta C ward, 56 individuals moved from Bokolo to Layin Garkuwa and 49 individuals from Gyazamar to Layin Bege in Dandume A ward, 54 individuals moved from Magaji Wondo Dansuda to Dandume in Dandume B ward and 25 individuals moved from Daddara to Fura Girke in Kusa ward. The incidents also resulted in 39 casualties, comprising 27 injuries and 12 fatalities. Following the incidents, Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) /f_ield staﬀ conducted rapid assessments on 9, 10, 12 and 14 August 2026 to inform the humanitarian community, as well as the government and partners, to enable a more targeted response. Non-food items (NFIs) and food were the most prevalent needs identi/f_ied. Other reported needs included shelter, health care, psychosocial support, transport, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and education. In Nigeria's north-west region, long-standing tensions between farmers and herders, as well as ethnic and religious groups, often lead to con/f_licts, attacks, and banditry or ‘hirabah’. These incidents involve kidnapping and theft along major highways. The crisis has intensi/f_ied in recent years, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-west regions. /reports/nigeria-north-west-nigeria-kebb.title: Nigeria — North-west Nigeria — Kebbi State Flash Report 271 (22 November 2025)
/reports/nigeria-north-west-nigeria-kebb.summary: On 22 November 2025, armed bandits attack was reported in the community of Maga in Danko ward of Danko/Wasagu local government area (LGA) in Kebbi State. This incident affected 548 individuals from 101 households, these included 313 children, 131 women, and 104 men. Key informants reported that 352 individuals from 60 households were displaced from the community of Maga to the community of Daki Takwas in Birnin Tudu ward of Gummi LGA, Zamfara State. Shelter, food, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) and non-food items (NFIs) were the most prevalent needs identified. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, alongside the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response. Nigeria's north-west region is increasingly affected by climate-related disasters, particularly seasonal flooding caused by heavy rainfall and riverbank/dam overflows. Nigeria's north-west region has had long-standing tensions between farmers and herders, as well as ethnic and religious groups, which often lead to conflicts, attacks, and banditry or 'hirabah'. These incidents involve kidnapping and theft along major highways. The crisis has intensified in recent years, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-west region.

A total of six injuries were reported. Shelter, food and non-food items (NFIs) were the most prevalent needs identified. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, alongside the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response. Nigeria's north-west region is increasingly affected by climate-related disasters, particularly seasonal flooding caused by heavy rainfall and riverbank/dam overflows. Nigeria’s north-west region has had long-standing tensions between farmers and herders, as well as ethnic and religious groups, which often lead to conflicts, attacks, and banditry or ‘hirabah’. These incidents involve kidnapping and theft along major highways. The crisis has intensified in recent years, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-west regions. /reports/nigeria-north-west-nigeria-zamf.summary: On 23 and 24 April 2026, armed bandit attacks occurred in the communities of Kurfan Danya, Faransi and Mai Zogo in Ruwan Jema Ward of Bukkuyum Local Government Area, and Keta in Kwaren Ganuwa Ward of Tsafe Local Government Area, Zamfara State. According to key informants, the attacks displaced 1,174 individuals from 237 households, including 655 children, 299 women, and 220 men. Of the displaced population, 414 individuals moved from Faransi, 325 from Mai Zogo, and 306 from Kurfan Danya to the community of Nasarawa Burkullo in Nasarawa Ward of Bukkuyum LGA, while 129 individuals were displaced from Keta to TsafeTown in Tsafe Ward of Tsafe LGA. A total of 27 casualties were reported, including 18 injuries and nine fatalities.

A total of nine injuries were reported and 112 shelters were affected by the windstorm.

pdf_text.text: Event Overview On 23 August 2026, an armed banditry and kidnapping incident occurred in Sauna community in Sauna R/Gora ward of Talata Mafara Local Government Area, Zamfara State. According to key informants, the incident displaced 531 individuals from 121 households, including 297 children, 217 adults, and 17 elderly persons. Of the displaced population, 531 individuals moved from Sauna community to Tsakkuwa community in Shiyar Galadima ward of Talata Mafara Local Government Area, where they are currently residing within the host community. A total of nine injuries were reported. Following the incident, Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments on 24 August 2026 to inform the humanitarian community, as well as the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response. Non-food items (NFIs), shelter and food were identified as priority needs. In Nigeria's north-west region, long-standing tensions between farmers and herders, as well as ethnic and religious groups, often lead to conicts, attacks, and banditry or ‘hirabah’. These incidents involve kidnapping and theft along major highways. The crisis has intensied in recent years, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-west regions. /reports/nigeria-north-west-sokoto-state.title: Nigeria — North-west — Sokoto State Flash Report 247 (30 July 2025)
/reports/nigeria-north-west-sokoto-state.summary: On 23 and 25 July 2025, floods and attacks by armed bandits were reported across two Local Government Areas (LGAs) in Sokoto State. The affected communities include Fajaldu, Wababe/Salau wards of the Dange/Shuni LGA and Lambar Tureta ward of the Tureta LGA. The attacks by armed bandits in Dange/Shuni LGA displaced 3,829 individuals (760 households) from the Fajaldu and Wababe/Salau wards; 1,562 individuals were displaced to Dange in Dange/Shuni LGA and 2,267 individuals were displaced to Lambar Tureta in Tureta LGA, all in Sokoto State. Additionally, flooding caused by heavy rainfall impacted 1,154 individuals (189 households), including 457 males and 697 females. The incident resulted in 42 casualties (8 fatalities and 27 injured), and 68 damaged shelters, affecting the living conditions of all the residents. The primary needs identified include food, shelter, and non-food items (NFIs). Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, as well as the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response.

pdf_text.text: Event Overview On 28 May 2025, armed bandits attacked the community of Tabkin Dawaki in Katuru ward of Shinkafi LGA in Zamfara State. The attack aﬀected 459 individuals across 91 households and displaced 25 individuals across 11 households to the Gidan Gona Camp in Shinkafi South ward. The aﬀected individuals included 257 children, 132 women, and 70 men. No casualties were recorded as a result of the incident. Food, non-food items (NFIs), security and shelter were identified as the most prevalent needs. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staﬀ conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. Nigeria’s north-west zone is aﬄicted with a multi-dimensional crisis. Long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups often result in attacks and banditry or hirabah. These attacks involve kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways by criminal groups. During the past years, the crisis accelerated and has resulted in widespread displacement across the north-west region. In addition to conflict-related crises, the region is increasingly aﬀected by climate-related disasters, particularly seasonal flooding caused by incessant heavy rainfall and riverbank/dam overflows. The attack affected 283 individuals across 56 households and displaced 58 individuals across 21 households to the community of Bakin Kasuwa in Bukkuyum ward, of the Bukkuyum LGA. The affected individuals included 159 children, 77 women, and 47 men. No injuries or fatalities were reported. Food, shelter and non-food items (NFIs) were identified as the most prevalent needs. Following these events, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community, alongside the government and partners, and to enable a more targeted response. Nigeria’s north-west zone is a site of ongoing crisis, characterised by long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups, often resulting in attacks and banditry or ‘hirabah’. These attacks involve kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways by criminal groups. In recent years, the crisis has accelerated, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-west region. In addition to conflict-related crises, the region is increasingly affected by climate-related disasters, particularly seasonal flooding caused by heavy rainfall and riverbank/dam overflows.

/reports/nigeria-north-westnorth-central.summary: Nigeria's North Central and North West Zones are afflicted with a multidimensional crisis that is rooted in long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups and involves attacks by criminal groups and banditry/hirabah (such as kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways). The crisis has accelerated during the past years because of the intensification of a?acks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region. On the evening of 18 October 2021, Goronyo town in Goronyo LGA was attacked by armed bandits. Following this event, a rapid assessment was conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) between 18 and 24 October 2021, identifying n estimated number of 389 individuals who were affected by the attack. 336 persons were displaced from Goronyo LGA towards Sokoto North LGA, both located in the state of Sokoto. Of the 336 individuals who were displaced, 104 persons were injured. An estimated 53 individuals lost their lives in the attack.

/reports/nigeria-north-westnorth-central.title: Nigeria — North West/North Central — Flash Report 74 (25—31 October 2021)
/reports/nigeria-north-westnorth-central.summary: Nigeria's North Central and North West Zones are afflicted with a multidimensional crisis that is rooted in long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups and involves attacks by criminal groups and banditry/hirabah (such as kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways). The crisis has accelerated during the past years because of the intensification of attacks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region. Between 25 and 31 October 2021, armed clashes between herdsmen and farmers; and bandits and local communities have led to new waves of population displacement. Following these events, rapid assessments were conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff with the purpose of informing the humanitarian community and government partners, and enable targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of affected populations. During the assessment period, the DTM identified an estimated number of 531 individuals who were displaced to neigbouring villages in the LGAs Zurmi in Zamfara State and Sabuwa in Katsina.

/reports/nigeria-plateau-intention-surve.title: Nigeria — Plateau - Intention Survey (August 2024)
/reports/nigeria-plateau-intention-surve.summary: To gain insight into the future intentions and aspirations of the IDPs in Plateau State, the DTM surveyed 15 LGAs where IDPs have been located. Out of the total 9,272 displaced households in the state, a sample of 1,326 was interviewed. Of these households, two per cent were residing in camps or camp-like settings, while the overwhelming majority, 98 per cent, were residing within host communities.

pdf_text.text: Nigeria north-west and north-central zone | Intention survey report Round 1 (August 2024) Benue Kogi Nasarawa Niger Plateau VOICES OF INTERNALLY DISPLACED PERSONS IN PLATEAU STATE NIGERIA INTENTION SURVEY AUGUST 2024 IOM Nigeria thanks the National Emergency Management Agency, Plateau State Emergency Management Agency, National Bureau of Statistics and the Nigerian Red Cross Society for their continued collaboration Nigeria north-west and north-central zone | Intention survey report Round 1 (August 2024) Fifty per cent (50%) of respondents in both camps/camp-like settings and in the host communities intend to return to their locations of origin. The major reason for this decision was re-occupy and re-possess assets and properties at their place of origin.. Forty-two per cent (42%) of respondents who intended to return to their locations of origin stated that their houses were partially damaged but can be repaired. INTENTIONS TO RETURN INTENTIONS TO RELOCATE INTENTIONS TO INTEGRATE Thirty-three per cent (33%) of respondents in Plateau State mentioned that they did not have the intention to leave the loca- tions where they are currently displaced in the coming months. They intend to integrate into the host communities. Seventy-two per cent (72%) of respondents who intended to integrate into the host community mentioned that the major reason for their decision was that the security situation was good in their current place of displacement. Only two per cent (2%) of respondents in north-west and north-central Nigeria had intention to relocate to another LGA or state, but most of this group intended to relocate to other LGAs in the state. T wenty-six per cent (26%) of respondents indicated that the search for economic opportunities and a means of livelihood was the major reason for the decision to relocate. OVERALL KEY FINDINGS IN PLATEAU STATE Nigeria north-west and north-central zone | Intention survey report Round 1 (August 2024) ROUND 1 III INTENTION SURVEY - NORTH CENTRAL NIGERIA PLATEAU STATE O BJECTIVES The Intention Survey tool aims at understanding IDPs' preferred solution options and the conditions that influenced such preferences. The main objectives of the survey are as follows: I. T o assess IDPs who wish to return, relocate, and locally integrate. II. T o map out areas to which IDPs wish to return, relocate, and locally integrate III. T o understand the conditions in (actual and intended) locations of solutions. IV. T o determine the estimated timelines for return, relocation, and local integration. INTRODUCTION Nigeria's north-central and north-western regions have been grappling with a complex crisis, rooted in long-standing ethno-social conflicts, which intensified in 2013 due to worsening socioeconomic and environmental conditions. The crisis encompasses deep-seated clashes between ethnic and linguistic groups, disputes between nomadic pastoralists and settled farmers, and violent criminal activities, including banditry and kidnappings along major highways. The situation escalated further in January 2018, leading to a surge in attacks that displaced hundreds of thousands of people. By the end of 2018, over a million individuals had been displaced. While some internally displaced persons (IDPs) have since returned, many remain unable to do so due to insecurity and fear of further attacks during their journey or after their return. The displacement crisis continues to affect the region. In response, the International Organization for Migration's (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM) and Protection sectors—alongside partners such as the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), State Emergency Management Agencies (SEMA), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), and others—conducted an assessment of IDPs' future intentions over the next 12 months. Supported by funding from BHA and ECHO, the survey aimed to evaluate whether displaced individuals in Plateau and nine other north-central and north- western states wished to return to their places of origin, integrate into their current communities, or relocate to new areas within or outside their state. From the 9,272 displaced households in Plateau, a sample of 1,326 households (90 in camps and 1,236 within host communities) was surveyed to understand their preferences for return, relocation, or integration over the next yea r. The main goals of this survey were to facilitate safe and dignified returns, support the integration of IDPs at their current locations, and assist with local relocations. By examining the factors influencing IDPs' decisions—such as security and livelihood opportunities—this report aims to enhance understanding of their decision-making processes. It also seeks to inform advocacy efforts, p olicy discussions, a nd protection-focused solutions for sustainable resettlement based on the IDPs' preferences. Nigeria north-west and north-central zone | Intention survey report Round 1 (August 2024) ROUND 1 IV IOM strictly followed the UN General Assembly Guidelines when planning and conducting this survey. While the UN General Assembly Guidelines are mainly addressed to states, they also explicitly apply to personal data files kept by governmental and international organizations, including IOM. The key principles of the guidelines are lawfulness and fairness, accuracy, interested- person access, non-discrimination, purpose-specification, proportionality, respect for the data subject’s rights, security and confidentiality, and accountability and supervision. The execution of this survey, including the methodology, scope, and presentation of the findings in this report, adhered to global best practices as outlined by the IOM Global DTM toolkit. Quantitative research methods were employed to formulate the interview questionnaire and implement the survey In preparation for the questionnaire, the CCCM/NFI/Shelter and the protection sectors were consulted. Following the consultations, DTM conducted 10 pilot interviews (5 households per population strata). The final survey questionnaire was comprised of eight (8) open-ended questions, 158 closed questions (closed questions are queries eliciting a “yes” or “no” response), and 17 semi-closed questions. After the finalization of the questionnaire, 35 enumerators and partners were trained by IOM DTM. Data was entered into the DTM KOBO server after a face- to-face interviews, which was then processed for the analytical report. Although the term “voluntary return” is not reflected in the questionnaire, interviewers were trained and instructed to explain to each interviewee that survey questions relate to returns of a voluntary nature only. The meaning of each solution—voluntary return, integration, and relocation was explained to each interviewee. DTM staff monitored interviews to verify that these concepts were clearly introduced and well understood. This survey, conducted in Plateau State, contributed to the analysis of the intention of the two surveyed population groups: IDPs dispersed in camp/camp-like settings: persons who have been forced to leave their homes or places of habitual residence and were residing in a formal or an informal camp. IDPs dispersed in host communities: persons who have been forced to leave their homes or places of habitual residence and were living with the local residents. The intention survey’s sampling framework relied on the DTM Mobility Tracking north-west and north-central Round 13 (March 2024) dataset . This data provided a breakdown of the IDP populations at administrative level 4 (location/sites), which formed the sample frame for the survey. The Intention Survey used a two-stage cluster sampling. The primary sampling units in the first stage were the IDP sites as identified by the Mobility Tracking Assessment Round 13. In the second stage, households were randomly interviewed from the identified IDP sites. INTENTION SURVEY - NORTH CENTRAL NIGERIA PLATEAU STATE METHODOLOGY

DTM NIGERIA: IOMNIGERIADTM@IOM.INT HTTPS://DISPLACEMENT.IOM.INT/NIGERIA - HTTPS://DTM.IOM.INT/NIGERIA DISPLACEMENT TRACKING MATRIX NIGERIA - NORTH-EAST ZONE RETURN INTENTION SURVEY BAKASSI CAMP - BORNO NOVEMBER 2021 In addition to the Return Intention Survey (RIS), three Focus Group Discussions (FGD) with members of the IDP population were organised in Bakassi Camp. The objective of these FGDs was to gain better insights into the dynamics of specific population categories in Bakassi Camp. The main outcome is that the majority of IDPs were not planning to leave Maiduguri Metropolitan Council (M.M.C.) LGA. Their main concerns in their LGAs or origin are accomodation and livelihood opportunities. Furthermore, many IDPs are convinced that there are better education opportunities in Maiduguri than in their LGAs of origin. l LIVELIHOOD FGD WITH MEN LIVELIHOOD FGD WITH WOMEN LIVELIHOOD FGD WITH YOUTH • Many men were reluctant to return to their LGAs of origin because of the lack of accommodation. Also, many of the locations of origin, especially in Marte LGA, remain inaccessible. The volatile security situation is a major challenge in regards to the return to locations of origin. • Other households do not know if their locations of origin are yet accessible. • Households originating from communities in Monguno LGA raised the concern of lack of accommodation and they reported that the rent is very expensive (2000 naira per room per month). As a result, many households plan to build a makeshift shelter in their location of origin. • Means of livelihood are also raised as a concern. Many IDPs used to be farmers before their displacement. They fear that they do not have the strength any longer to work on their lands after all these years in displacement and they doubt having similar access to their farmlands. Additionally, they said the package offered by the governor, ( 100,000 naira per household) is not sufficient for their transportation to their LGAs of origin, to buy food and allow them to start sustainable employment. • Many households wish to remain because in Maiduguri there are better education opportunities for their children compared to their LGAs of origin. • Most households originating from Monguno believe that farming around Monguno Town is now possible. Furthermore, the route between Monguno – Baga is accessible and they hope that the parameters for farmlands will be extended. • Many women reported that they don’t have a choice other than to respect their husband’s decision. • Many of the female heads of households intend to leave because life in Maiduguri is more expensive compared to their LGA of origin. They prefer to return to their LGA of origin where they can start a petty business and count on the support of relatives. • Many of the youth were undecided. The majority mentioned that they would respect the decision made by their parents. The married ones prefer to stay in Maiduguri as there are more livelihood opportunities. • In Maiduguri, there are livelihood opportunities with petty trading and little jobs. They fear that there will be no way to sustain themselves and their families in their locations of origin. • Many prefer to remain in the location of displacement until they are assured that their locations of origin are safe to return to.

DURABLE SOLUTION SOCIO-ECONOMIC SURVEY - DAUCHI SETTLEMENT This report provides an in-depth look at the progress made in supporting the displaced residents of the Dauchi settlement, located in Song local government area, Adamawa State. Dauchi, home to over 200 households, has become a permanent refuge for people who were forced to flee their homes due to the insurgency in north-east Nigeria. Instead of returning to their areas of origin, many displaced persons have chosen to integrate into this local community. Through a detailed survey, this report explores the living conditions and livelihoods of Dauchi’s residents while also assessing the availability of key infrastructure and services, such as health centres, schools, and water sources. In addition, demographic data from registration exercises offers valuable insights into the population’s age and gender distribution, which helps inform future interventions for the community. The findings provide a comprehensive view of Dauchi’s socio-economic landscape and the challenges its residents face, making this report a vital resource for those working to improve conditions and provide long-term solutions for the settlement’s residents. INTRODUCTION METHODOLOGY The methodology employed in this report was designed to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the conditions in the Dauchi settlement and to assess the progress made towards achieving durable solutions for displaced residents. The methodology is based on the following key components: A socio-economic survey was conducted on 30 August 2024 to gather detailed information on the livelihood, economic status, and living conditions of the households in the Dauchi settlement. The survey targeted 165 households, ensuring a broad and representative sample of the community’s population. Trained enumerators administered structured questionnaires to collect data on income sources, employment status, household expenditures, food security, and coping mechanisms. The data gathered from the survey provided a reliable basis for understanding the economic activities, challenges, and opportunities within the settlement. A facility mapping exercise evaluated the availability and functionality of critical infrastructure and services within the settlement. This assessment involved a systematic review of key facilities such as health centres, public facilities, schools, and water supply systems. The goal was to determine the number of each facility and the extent to which these services met the needs of the residents and to identify gaps in service provision. The facility data was collected through site visits and consultations with local authorities and service providers. The data from the biometric registrations were also used to profile the community in Dauchi. The registration exercise from July to September 2024, captured 100 per cent of the settlement’s population. This registration process involved collecting of biometric data (fingerprints and photographs) to ensure accurate identification and record-keeping of each resident. The biometric registration has generated a database of all individuals in the community, which can be used for future assistance programs, resource allocation, and demographic planning. The process ensured inclusivity by capturing every resident, regard- less of age or gender. In collaboration with the National Population Commission, an additional registration exercise was conducted, specifically targeting children under 10. This exercise provided critical demographic information on the younger population in the Dauchi settlement. The data obtained helped identify age and gender distribution patterns and assess the vulnerability of children in the community, which is essential for planning child-focused interventions and services. The data collected from the socio-economic survey, facility mapping, and registration exercises were analysed to generate insights into the living conditions, socio-economic status, and access to services in Dauchi settlement. Quantitative data from the surveys and registrations were analyzed using statistical software to identify trends, challenges, and areas of progress. Qualitative data from facility mapping and consultations were analyzed to assess the quality of services and infrastructure available to the residents. A 4 SEP 2024 PROGRESS TOWARDS DURABLE SOLUTION SOCIO-ECONOMIC SURVEY - DAUCHI SETTLEMENT While the methodology provided robust and comprehensive data, certain limitations should be noted. First, due to the absence of some representative of the head of household/member of the household who went to the farm, not all households in the settlement were surveyed. However, over 60 per cent of the households participated, providing a solid representative sample. Additionally, facility mapping relied on observational data and consultations, which may be subject to interpretational bias. However, these limitations were mitigated by triangulating data from different sources to ensure accuracy and reliability. This methodological approach enabled the report to offer a holistic understanding of the conditions in the Dauchi settlement, focusing on socio-economic factors, demographic trends, and service availability. The data collected and analysed through this rigorous process is a foundation for making informed recommendations and planning future interventions to improve displaced residents’ lives. LIMITATIONS
